title: Maybe Donald Trump Doesn’t Want His Party to Win the Midterms
excerpt: I put it to you plainly: Would someone who wanted to win the midterms be behaving as Donald Trump has? We are a full 20 minutes into Trump’s address to the nati
body: I put it to you plainly: Would someone who wanted to win the midterms be behaving as Donald Trump has? We are a full 20 minutes into Trump’s address to the nation, on the day before Election Day, and he has yet to pivot from pipes
He is standing beside, of all things, the Reflecting Pool, and he is talking about, of all things, the pipes

With visual aids, prepared in advance, lest anyone say “Surely this was some mistake!” (It was some mistake, but, like so many Trump-era mistakes, it was a mistake that had been planned.) He is reflecting on the lifespan of grass. (“Like the human being, grass has a life also.”) Will someone tell him that something big is happening in the country tomorrow? Here he stands, for his closing remarks to the American people
And those closing remarks are overwhelmingly about the Reflecting Pool
As he speaks, he holds up his slides, each of which he describes with the beleaguered energy of an old laptop with too many open tabs
He goes on about the vandals with box cutters and knives (there were no vandals with box cutters and knives) who attacked the pool

Look, if I wanted to win the midterms, and I were Donald Trump, I would not go stand in front of the physical symbol of my failure and remind people that my chosen team installed its lining so badly that it looked like the work of vandals with box cutters, but that is just me
I am not Donald Trump for numerous reasons
I enjoy hugging my family and often admit that I was wrong
I am not Narcissus-levels of obsessed with a reflective body of water

If I had been as embroiled in an unsuccessful pool renovation as Donald Trump has, you could not drag me to the pool with wild horses, not even next to a nifty little prepared sign with a picture of the pool that reads: Back, and more beautiful than ever! Maybe he is trying to spin the “blue wave” as something positive that he has done to remove algae from the Reflecting Pool? I could not tell you

Maybe he thinks that if he can just clean the pool enough, everyone will look into it and see the reflection that he sees? If I were Donald Trump and I wanted to win the midterms, I wouldn’t march from state to state demanding to be remembered
This is like if the albatross around your neck thought it was helping

The best that can be said of his Reflecting Pool speech is that it included no odes to anyone’s posterior, not that of Jon Husted or Nicki Minaj or even Abraham Lincoln, who might have sprung to mind because he was seated so near
And that there was only one joke about renaming the reflecting pool the Trump Reflecting Pool (which was a joke, I think)
Of course, I do not want to imply that the speech lacked any of the president’s usual transphobic, bigoted scaremongering about “mutilization” and “jihadists.” Those were also there

But I am not sure that someone standing in front of the worst metaphor for his presidency and sleepily saying that “communist jihadists” (how does this combination of beliefs work, exactly, in his mind?) are coming to take the Senate is the winning closer he pictured

Nor is his announcement that a deal with Iran “could happen.” (Anything could happen!) Or his bewildering statement that the “Green New Scam” predicted that we would all be dead in 12 years? “Here we are, we’re not dead.” Got it

Clear as the … now-at-least-temporarily-algae-free pool surface! If I were Donald Trump and I wanted to win the midterms, I would certainly not go stand in front of the Reflecting Pool and say any of this
Maybe, instead, I would go hide in a deep hole and hope that no one remembered I existed or noticed anything I had done

title: Trump’s Venezuela Project Just Got a Lot More Complicated
excerpt: T wo days after María Corina Machado’s high-stakes return to Venezuela last week, she walked into her low-slung party headquarters, which had been raided and va
body: T wo days after María Corina Machado’s high-stakes return to Venezuela last week, she walked into her low-slung party headquarters, which had been raided and vandalized by supporters of the regime that had forced her into exile
The graffiti had been painted over and the debris had been cleared
Machado was there for her first major meeting back in Caracas, with about 100 family members of political prisoners
Machado could see that many held photos of their detained relatives
Many also wore shirts that read Libertad. “They persecute the innocent using all the power of the state,” Machado said in a speech
She didn’t mention names, but everyone in the crowd knew that she was referring to the cadre of leaders now running the country under U.S. tutelage

Still being held were at least 400 political prisoners, according to civil-society groups, people Machado referred to as “our absolute priority” and “our heroes.” Eglis Manaure was in the small crowd, holding a photo of her husband, Enrique Nauris Parada, one of the 400

Listening to Machado speak, Manaure thought not only of the prospect that her husband might finally be freed, but also that his jailers might soon be punished. “Whatever form of justice she”—meaning Machado—“decides,” Manaure told us after the meeting

In the days following her return, Machado has begun talking about justice, reparations, and the “dismantling of the repressive state.” Put another way: One U.S. ally in Venezuela appears to be calling for the prosecution of another
It is an early glimpse into the rivalry the United States will now have to manage as it oversees Venezuela’s democratic transition

For 10 months, ever since what President Trump described today as the “conquest of Venezuela,” the administration has consolidated power around a single pliant figure: Interim President Delcy Rodríguez

Through Rodríguez, the U.S. was able to negotiate an opaque petroleum agreement that Trump, in a dubious claim, has called “the biggest oil deal in world history.” (Trump, in another dubious claim, said today that “we’re taking in hundreds of billions of dollars of oil.”) In a January interview with The Atlantic , he said of Rodríguez: “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price.” But as of last week, the U.S. is no longer ruling over a unipolar Venezuela
Machado is by far the most popular figure in Venezuelan politics
In recent days, her supporters have crowded highways and plazas and churches across parts of the country to get a look at the returned leader
Last Tuesday, while Machado met with the families of political prisoners, Rodríguez held her own rally, where she danced on a stage to popular songs—a stunt that was widely mocked by Venezuelans

And yet it was Rodríguez, watching her power come under threat, who derided Machado’s return as a “show.” In its first 10 months running Venezuela, the Trump administration chose to work with vestiges of Nicolás Maduro’s regime—ostensibly in the name of stability and economic growth—instead of prioritizing a rapid democratic transition
It appeared to discourage, if not outright block, Machado’s return
That approach simplified the challenge of steering a foreign country, allowing Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Trump to extract what they wanted from Rodríguez
There was no democratic structure to build, no immediate quest for accountability, no need to mediate among competing political factions

The State Department argued that it was supporting incremental reforms that were more likely to stick, and said that a hasty appearance by Machado could cause government institutions and the country’s military to split

But all the while, anger was growing among Venezuelans who had celebrated the removal of Maduro in January. “What Trump has done so far was the easy part,” Steven Levitsky, a professor of Latin American studies at Harvard, told us. “Pushing an authoritarian clique out of power is the hard part
It’s going to take a complex negotiation.” [ From the December 2026 issue: What the U.S. is really doing in Venezuela ] Machado’s return has hastened that negotiation

Last Monday, a senior State Department official told journalists that, as part of the Trump administration’s three-phase plan for Venezuela’s return to democracy, Rodríguez would need to declare a “permanent vacancy in the presidency” once electoral reforms are completed, triggering a six-month period before new elections can occur
This process is highly likely to result in a Machado presidency by mid- to late 2027, at the earliest

Machado’s team has already begun pushing to speed up the pace, knowing that dragging out the process could erode her position. “Machado is operating on a very tight timeline,” Paul Angelo, a Latin America expert who was previously at the Defense Department and is now at the consultancy McLarty Associates, told us. “She’s the most popular character in the country, but she’s also someone whose cachet as the leader of a unified opposition likely has its limits.” N either the United States nor Machado has articulated a postelection plan for Rodríguez and the rest of the Maduro regime should Machado win
There are no easy options: The United States, or another country, could offer them safe haven

Or they could remain in Venezuela, subject to prosecution—the preference of most Machado supporters. “The ideal is that the Venezuelan courts themselves, the Venezuelan justice system itself, can try and convict those responsible for human-rights abuses,” Martha Tineo, a co-founder of Justicia, Encuentro y Perdón, which tracks forced detentions in Venezuela, told us. “No political agreement of any kind can be above justice.” The reality is more complicated
If Rodríguez is to remain in power though the elections, potentially standing as a candidate, she will almost certainly want an assurance that she won’t be jailed after the vote
The same is true for much of her regime, including top military and police officials who have committed well-documented human-rights abuses
But the prospect of impunity is abhorrent to Machado’s supporters
Bridging that divide now falls on the United States

Those involved in the democratic transition—reforming and rebuilding Venezuela’s judicial and electoral systems—believe that Washington has the final say over their work. “This whole process originated with a green light from the United States,” one Venezuelan working on the transition told us. [ Read: Why Venezuela? ] Trump’s oil deal could also be complicated by Machado’s return and the restoration of a political opposition in Venezuela

Most of Machado’s supporters believe that the deal is unconstitutional and could be canceled once an independent judiciary is established. (The Trump administration hasn’t released many details about the deal, but has said it was structured to endure over time.) Although Machado had been trying to remain in the White House’s good graces, at her first press conference in Caracas, on Thursday, she said that the agreement “does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants.” I n Rubio’s telling , he cautioned Machado only once against coming back to Venezuela
That was immediately after the devastating June earthquake
At the time, he told reporters last week, the administration was exclusively concerned about ensuring the delivery of aid and feared that her arrival could derail those efforts

Several weeks ago, Rubio said, the Trump administration warned Rodríguez’s government that Machado had a right to make her widely anticipated return, clearing the way for it to happen. “We spoke to the interim authorities and just said, ‘Look, our expectation is that she’s a Venezuelan; she belongs in her country,’” Rubio said. “She should be allowed to return, and she should be allowed to return unperturbed.” Rubio has said that the administration will measure Rodríguez’s actions, rather than her rhetoric about its gradual road map for transitioning to an elected government

The map includes plans announced after the most recent round of transition talks among regime figures and a subset of opposition groups, aimed at reforming the country’s highest court and electoral body

Rubio has been open in acknowledging the administration’s willingness to use the threat of reimposing sanctions on Venezuela’s oil sector, or on leaders such as Rodríguez and other senior members of her government, as a coercive tool to avoid foot-dragging. “No matter what people say along the way, as long as it happens, this is a results-based process,” Rubio said. “So far, frankly, on everything we’ve asked for in this process, be it the economic reforms, the political reforms—it’s happening.” [ Read: Venezuela seems to be going … well? ] Administration officials have voiced periodic frustration with Machado, who they have suggested has at times been impractical and perhaps too willing to compromise stability and economic growth in pursuit of democratic ideals
A State Department spokesperson told us that Machado’s party, Vente Venezuela, had been invited to this month’s transition talks in Caracas but did not attend

Rubio’s plans for Venezuela are nested within a larger Latin America strategy predicated around three interlinked goals: building American commercial primacy by accruing new business deals that squeeze out Chinese firms in the process; defeating drug cartels, using visa sanctions, terror-group designations, and the Pentagon’s militarized partnerships with countries such as Ecuador and Colombia; and choking off illegal migration

title: Who Thought This Ad Was a Good Idea?
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture

Who says the Midwest is boring? On this election eve, the two most bizarre stories in politics are both coming out of Senate races in what’s sometimes derided as “flyover country.” But as those of us from the region know, low topography doesn’t mean low drama
In Michigan, Democratic Representative Haley Stevens—the runner-up in this summer’s primary for a U.S
Senate seat—went literally overnight from grudgingly backing the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed to endorsing the Republican Mike Rogers, as my colleague Jonathan Chait reported

Here we’d customarily explain the reason for her abrupt shift, but Stevens herself couldn’t or wouldn’t articulate that during an excruciating 15-minute interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper. (A follow-up with The Free Press wasn’t clarifying either.) If El-Sayed loses and Democrats fail to capture a Senate majority, the commotion over Stevens’s flip will appear pivotal
If, however, Republicans lose control of the Senate, then the eye-popping closing ad by Roger Marshall of Kansas, a GOP incumbent, will be a good symbol of where things went wrong for Republicans
A key issue in the race has been reporting about how Marshall sued more than 700 patients over medical bills
Some paid interest rates as high as 18 percent; 81 arrests were made in relation to medical debt, according to The New York Times
Experts told the paper that such suits are very rare
In an election in which the affordability of basic services is a key issue, these cases have been a millstone around Marshall’s neck, and some polls show him trailing the Democrat Adam Hamilton

Saturday evening, a Kansas City radio host posted a new Marshall ad , featuring the candidate speaking directly to the camera, that apparently aims to turn that around. “When I practiced as a small-town OB doc, often practicing as the only OB in the middle of 40,000 people, my wife and I decided to take care of everyone, regardless of their ability to pay,” he says. “Now to ensure that 40,000 Kansans would still have access to care, we did have to keep the lights on, so we occasionally handed some accounts over to collection agencies.” An old political maxim says that “if you’re explaining, you’re losing,” pointing to the importance of not being on the defensive

If that’s true, what does it mean if you’re explaining that you sent hundreds of your constituents to debt collectors over medical bills? The desire to defend oneself against attacks is understandable—though a disciplined candidate doesn’t take bait—but Marshall isn’t even disputing the crux of the attack against him
The idea that a candidate would use his final message of the campaign to broadcast these facts to voters is shocking
His own aides agreed, according to the Times

The paper reported that the senator proposed the ad about two weeks ago, but advisers said it was a bad idea, and that Marshall should “contrast his record with Adam Hamilton, his Democratic rival, especially on immigration.” Instead, Marshall hired a film crew and taped the spot himself, not telling some of his staff

When they found out, they again opposed spending any campaign funds to air it, so Marshall personally started sending it to people outside the campaign. “I would have been glad to put it out much, much sooner,” Marshall told The Wall Street Journal
Determining what effect it has on the outcome of the race will probably be impossible, but the debacle shows what makes Marshall such a weak candidate
He should be a shoo-in for reelection: He’s a doctor, he’s got a good head of hair, and he’s a Republican in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932
When his colleague Jerry Moran ran for reelection, in an underwhelming year for Republicans, he won by 23 percentage points
But Marshall is battling for his career in a race considered a toss-up
The latest Times poll shows Hamilton up 5 percentage points
A Washington Post poll was even more dramatic, showing the Democrat leading by 9 points
The Kansas race demonstrates some of the reasons this election has been so difficult for the GOP
First, Republicans have some weak candidates
Marshall is not very dynamic, is vulnerable to attacks, and evidently has bad political instincts
Second, Democrats have several unusually strong candidates
Hamilton is a charismatic megachurch pastor
Third, GOP voters—such as the ones who have made Kansas a rock-ribbed Republican state for so long—are unenthusiastic and demotivated
An Emerson College poll found the state’s approval of President Trump underwater, at 45–51, and other polls have similar results
High fuel prices have been a big issue in Kansas , a heavily agricultural state
Even with all of this, Marshall could win
If he does, it will be a testament to the power of a state’s long record of GOP allegiance to outweigh even an awful campaign
And if he doesn’t win and returns to practicing medicine, prospective patients have been warned about how he handles billing

title: The Anger Election’s Final Twist
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Over the weekend, in a November surprise, Democratic Representative Haley Stevens,
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Over the weekend, in a November surprise, Democratic Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan primary for U.S
Senate, appeared at Bishop Marvin Winans’s church in Detroit alongside the Republican candidate, Mike Rogers

She endorsed him soon after, but insisted that she was “not turning my back on Democrats.” Her endorsement sparked anger among Democrats, who argued that even a vote for Rogers is as good as support for President Trump and his policy agenda—but an endorsement of Rogers is, as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer put it , a “despicable betrayal.” Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, returned only a small barb as he tried to stay on message: “I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he told a gaggle of reporters. “This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from their government
I’m a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not” Stevens and Rogers
Many of those voters have been clear about their concerns: They want the government to be less corrupt ; they want everyday items to be more affordable; they want an end to the war in Iran
On this week’s episode, my colleagues Gabby Deutch and David A
Graham join me to discuss the issues on voters’ minds as they head into the voting booth, and what the officials they elect can actually do to make them better

The following is a transcript of the episode: Gabby Deutch: I was just in in Pennsylvania, and I chatted with a couple of college students at East Stroudsburg University, a small school in the Poconos, and they were two guys who had voted for Trump two years ago, and they said, He promised he wouldn’t get us into any more wars, and now our fraternity brother just shipped out to the Middle East
And it’s not just about the issues; it’s a sense of feeling lied to
I’m Adam Harris, and the election is finally here
The weekend featured a rare November surprise in Michigan, and candidates who’ve been barnstorming their districts and states for months made their final arguments to voters

My colleagues, Atlantic staff writers Gabby Deutsch and David Graham, joined me to discuss why corruption might be a winning message, how young voters are feeling, and which candidates seem to be delivering actual policy proposals that resonate

But before we get to questions, I want to remind you that tomorrow, November 3, Radio Atlantic co-host Hanna Rosin and I will be hosting an Election Night livestream starting at 9 p.m.eastern time , where we’ll discuss results and the ideas driving the nation
We got a rare November surprise over the weekend when Haley Stevens, the Democratic primary challenger to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed the Republican Senate candidate, Mike Rogers
Can you just sort of walk us through: What happened there? Deutch: I think that’s the question that we’re still trying to really find the answer to, in a certain extent
But Haley Stevens lost the Senate primary, of course, to El-Sayed in a pretty close and rather contentious race
It seemed pretty clear over the last few months that they were not the best of friends, to put it mildly, but she did endorse him in the Democratic ticket
Over the last week, things have heated up a bit
There was an ad that came out, not from El-Sayed’s campaign, but promoting him
Harris: Yeah, let’s talk about that ad for a second
It’s from an outside group, and it tries to tie the high cost of groceries to America’s military support for Israel
Deutch: And Haley Stevens called on him to condemn that more strongly than he did
But through all of it, she said she was still standing by her support for him
And then in the last 48-ish hours, there was a bunch of action on that front
They were going to campaign together, the two of them, at a unity rally in Detroit
And then Haley Stevens put out this statement
She was still saying she was endorsing him
And then on Sunday morning, we woke up and saw that Haley Stevens was at church with Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee
I think the question of what exactly changed overnight is still pretty open, and I think all of the campaign reporters in the country are trying to find the answer
But yeah, now we have the loser in the Democratic primary for Senate endorsing the Republican
Harris: I guess my question out of that, right—because but you mentioned, right, she’s a loser in the Democratic primary; she’s an outgoing congresswoman at this point
It seemed that Democrats pretty quickly coalesced around, kind of, condemning her endorsement

So does this actually change anything outside of her vote and her support? Deutch: There is a contingent of some Jewish Democrats and pro-Israel Democrats within Michigan who, since the primary—people who had supported Stevens’s campaign said that they were not going to support El-Sayed
Some said they were going to sit the race out
So that’s been, you know, kind of a small force happening throughout the election
I’m not sure that Stevens making the decision to endorse Rogers really grows it
It’s already been building, kind of, organically in a section of the Jewish community that’s unhappy with El-Sayed’s language about Israel and Zionism and some Jewish-aligned issues
But, you know, I think we’ve seen from the Rogers campaign—they’re obviously very excited about this and hoping that if there are people who are still on the fence at this point
And El-Sayed and Rogers are pulling—El-Sayed seems to be in the lead, but it’s closer than in the governor’s race in Michigan as well

So if there were holdouts who were looking for a sign, I think maybe, you know, for that handful of people who could be relevant—or who could be decisive—that is, you know, they think perhaps this is the thing that does it

The night before, the Milwaukee County executive’s hometown Brewers won the World Series for the first time in their 56-year existence
A new poll released the same day found Crowley to be in a strong position to make his own history next week, by becoming the first Black governor of Wisconsin

But it was an even bigger potential victory that prompted Crowley, wearing a Brewers pullover and sneakers the color of Wisconsin cheddar, to declare to the crowd: “This is where I get a little giddy!” Democrats in Wisconsin have begun to imagine that they can not only retain the governorship but also capture control of both chambers of the state legislature for the first time since 2008. “Think about what we’re going to be able to do with that,” Crowley told the crowd of students who cheered the possibility
Such a sweep would cap a remarkable comeback for Democrats in Wisconsin, a swing state at the presidential level where, until recently, Republicans have maintained a tight grip on the legislature
Unified government would allow Democrats to undo a raft of conservative policies first enacted by former Governor Scott Walker and reverse years of budget cuts imposed by GOP lawmakers
The Democrats’ drive for a trifecta in Wisconsin is part of a broader effort to take maximum advantage of what seems to be one of their most favorable national electoral environments in decades

They have a chance to win full control in states including Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Minnesota while cutting into Republican majorities in many others. “We’re looking at what could be a generational shift in state legislative power,” Heather Williams, the president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, told me

Sweeps at the state level could yield more immediate policy changes than even Democratic victories in the battle for control of Congress, because a split federal government would likely result in legislative gridlock during President Trump’s final two years in office

Full Democratic control in more states could also upend the nationwide redistricting wars, giving the party fresh opportunities to counter Trump’s red-state gerrymandering push. [ Read: Redistricting isn’t going as Republicans planned ] For years, Republicans devoted far more attention and money to state legislative races than Democrats did

In 2010, that focus paid off when a GOP wave during President Obama’s first term not only swept Republicans into the House majority but helped them flip 20 state legislative chambers across the country

Democrats have spent years playing catch-up, trying—occasionally in vain—to convince a donor base obsessed with presidential politics that spending money on cheaper but less sexy downballot races is a more cost-effective investment

In early 2019, I wrote about an organization called Future Now , one of a constellation of Democratic groups that formed with a focus on building state-level power in the aftermath of Trump’s first win
At the time, Future Now was hoping to spend about $10 million to help Democrats flip state legislative races in 2020
The group has since changed its name to the States Project, and it has raised $100 million to spend this year. “So we’ve made a lot of progress,” its co-founder Daniel Squadron told me

But he noted that Republicans are still outspending Democrats in many states, which could limit the party’s gains: “I do believe that we are leaving seats on the table.” Nowhere has the Democrats’ renewed focus on state power proved more consequential than in Wisconsin, where a years-long drive to loosen the GOP’s stranglehold on the legislature has resembled a slow-motion game of dominoes
A decade ago, Republicans held the governorship and near-supermajorities in the legislature

In 2018, Tony Evers narrowly ousted Republican Governor Scott Walker, and that same year, Democrats began chipping away at the conservative majority on the state supreme court through a series of judicial elections that drew tens of millions of dollars in spending from both sides
In 2023, liberals won a majority on the court, which soon overturned the Republican-drawn legislative map after ruling that its jumble of disconnected territory violated the state constitution
New district lines took effect for the 2024 election, and even though Trump narrowly carried Wisconsin over Kamala Harris, Democrats picked up seats in the state Senate and assembly
Those wins, in turn, put them in position to seek a trifecta this year
W isconsin Democrats kept gaining momentum as 2026 began
The new, fairer legislative maps prompted a slew of longtime Republican incumbents to retire rather than face much tougher reelection bids
And they attracted stronger Democratic candidates, such as Trevor Jung, the 30-year-old director of transit for Racine, a deindustrialized city on the shores of Lake Michigan

Jung, who previously served on Racine’s city council, is campaigning for an open state-Senate seat that could determine which party holds the majority. “This is the tipping point,” Jung told me last week

We were sitting inside the local Democratic headquarters, where a cardboard cutout of a smiling Barack Obama behind a podium served as a reminder of the party’s last, brief run of dominance in Wisconsin. (Obama carried the state by nearly 14 points in 2008, a landslide by Wisconsin standards that helped Democrats win majorities in the legislature as well.) When I asked Jung whether he would have run in the old version of his district, which contained less of Racine and more deep-red rural areas, he laughed in a way that suggested the question was a bit foolish. “No,” he replied. “That is how bad these gerrymandered maps were
It was crazy.” Jung has been the beneficiary of good fortune before

Born in Krasnodar, a Russian city across the Black Sea from Crimea, he was a 2-year-old orphan when a gay hairstylist looking to start a family in Racine flew almost halfway across the world to adopt him

Had he grown up as part of the underclass in Vladimir Putin’s Russia, Jung reflected, “I very much would have been part of the war machine now.” Instead, he was raised in a blue-collar section of Racine, and when he returned to the city after studying urban affairs in college, he saw the effect of years of austerity budgets imposed by the GOP-controlled legislature

Cuts in state funding have forced local governments across Wisconsin to hold repeated referenda to raise property taxes just to keep schools open and maintain municipal services, including police departments. “There has just been a concerted effort from legislative Republicans to go after areas that Democrats live in,” Jung said, “so that they don’t have the political power of a growing, successful population
That has been their approach.” That has continued, he said, even though Wisconsin has had, in Evers, a Democratic governor for the past eight years
Evers has described himself as “the goalie,” using his veto power to hold back the Republican legislature
With majorities in the assembly and the Senate, Jung argued, Democrats would be able to play offense instead of defense

Jung told me he’s been volunteering for Democratic campaigns since Obama’s first election—when he was 12 years old—and that the vibe he’s encountered while knocking doors this time is distinct from years past. “People are just so sick of the way that politicians have treated voters, with the way that government has been ineffective, with the drama and the craziness out of Washington,” Jung said
When he tells people he’s a Democrat, often the response is I’m going Democrat this year . “You hear the words this year , and you catch it, and you’re like, ‘Okay
State legislative campaigns have traditionally been low-budget operations, a contest of which candidate can knock on more doors and turn out more voters
But as spending on these races has surged, they’re beginning to resemble hard-fought congressional campaigns, complete with dueling negative ads on TV
Republicans are running ads calling Jung “Tricky Trevor” and accusing him of campaigning on the public dime while serving as Racine’s transit director (a charge that Jung laughed off)
About a half hour’s drive north of Racine, I met with Dan Bukiewicz, the longtime mayor of Oak Creek, who is running to flip a Republican-held seat in the state assembly
As in Racine, the GOP incumbent decided not to seek another term

title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
excerpt: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization
body: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization
Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights
But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired
Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement
And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed
DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics
Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage

This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business
Some key findings from the report include the following: Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver
On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business
That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago
But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses
Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage
At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average
In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business
The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall
The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights
Insufficient context reduces insight quality
When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives
Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%
Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context
Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness
At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon
Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive
Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights
The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%)
They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%)
The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents
Download the report This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff
It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: Stop counting tokens, start counting what ships
excerpt: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once
body: When a developer gives an AI agent a coding task, the agent does more than answer once
It plans, generates code, runs tests, and repeats the process to correct errors
A single task can use 10 to 50 times more tokens than a basic chat prompt
The more useful the agent becomes, the more calls it makes
With per-token pricing, the workflows creating the most value can also become the most expensive
The financial pressure is already visible
Uber reportedly exhausted its entire 2026 AI budget by April after expanding its use of Claude Code
GitHub Copilot moved from flat-rate pricing to metered credits
Gartner predicts that AI coding token costs will surpass average developer salaries by 2028
The natural response is rationing usage caps, seat limits, and approvals before developers launch agents
But blanket limits can restrict the workflows delivering value
Cost per token measures consumption, not results
Some spending reflects waste, including retries and runaway loops
Some represents the work of shipping software
A meter cannot distinguish them, and neither can a spending cap
Measure the software that ships A better measure is cost per merged pull request: total AI-assisted development cost divided by the number of changes that pass review and are merged
Track rework and defects alongside it so cheaper changes do not conceal lower quality
If that cost falls as AI usage rises, without compromising quality, developers are converting more consumption into useful software
The question is not how many tokens they use, but how much finished work the investment produces
Improving that equation requires two changes: reserve expensive inference for tasks that need it, and lower the cost of routine work
Match the model to the task Agentic coding does not require the most powerful model at every step
Use a frontier model, or an on-premises flagship when policy requires it, for difficult planning and novel reasoning
Route suitable work, including code generation, test creation, and repeated refactoring, to open-weight models you operate yourself
A gateway can route requests according to task complexity, data sensitivity, cost, and latency
This reserves premium inference for the moments that justify it rather than applying premium pricing to an entire workflow
Open-weight models make this division increasingly practical
Software-engineering benchmarks show that leading open-weight models can approach frontier performance on some tasks
That does not establish equivalence across every repository or workflow
Evaluate candidates against your own code, tests, and acceptance criteria before assigning production work
Change the economics of repeated use Next, decide who owns the capacity
With rented inference, every call adds to the bill
With owned capacity, most of the cost is committed upfront, so each additional call gets cheaper as usage grows
The economics are simple: per-token pricing makes heavy use more expensive, while owned capacity becomes more efficient as teams use it more
Power, operations, maintenance, and depreciation all must be considered
The number that matters is the fully loaded cost per merged pull request
Owned capacity also delivers a type of value that never appears on an invoice: control over sensitive code
When code generation and testing run on-premises, proprietary code stays inside the enterprise
Only approved planning prompts and governed exceptions go to external models, through a gateway the organization controls
That opens the sensitive repositories where security usually stalls adoption, and where the biggest gains are waiting
Test the operating model At HPE, a hybrid AI platform routes routine workloads from more than 150 internal applications to open-weight models running on premises, including on HPE Private Cloud AI

title: The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

The agentic web is here In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves
But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality
They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts
This new era is being called the agentic web
It will inevitably transform the internet—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess

Find out how AI agents are transforming the internet, and what we stand to lose in the process . —Grace Huckins Are we there yet? Eliminating traffic deaths Every year, traffic crashes kill more than 1 million people worldwide
They’re also the leading cause of death for children and young adults
Cheap, proven ways to make roads safer exist, including tightening intersections with planters and lowering speed limits
But government logjams and red tape can make it difficult to roll out these changes
Still, some cities are making impressive progress by investing in public transit, extending curbs, and using cameras to spot danger zones in need of a redesign

Here’s how close we are to eradicating traffic deaths . —Sara Kiley Watson This story is the final part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter

title: The agentic web is here
excerpt: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision
body: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision

Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves

To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.  At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections
But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized

New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online

Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web
This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control
As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess

For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services

And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out

Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers

They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus.  They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online

Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight.  As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good
Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them
Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services
Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience
Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use
Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift
And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not

How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla

But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.” Building a web for agents There are two ways to approach building the agentic web
The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to
The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media
That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers

When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says
Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces

The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill
We humans are naturals at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not
PINGNAN LU So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach
In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do
Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways

For example, if you open up Claude, ChatGPT, or Muse, you’ll find an option to add a wide variety of “plug-ins” or “connectors” that your agents can use: Gmail connectors allow your agent to triage your inbox, and Instacart plug-ins let your agent do your grocery shopping
Under the hood, these plug-ins allow your agent to interact with the back ends of websites using text commands
When human engineers design these plug-ins, they can decide how they want to allow agents to interact with the website—and what they don’t want to let them do
In this way, connectors can help make agents much safer online
For instance, Muse can buy products for you using its connector with Stripe’s Link payment service

Stripe knows your credit card number, but the agent doesn’t see it, and the connector requires human confirmation before a purchase goes through—so Muse can’t go on an unlicensed shopping spree.  Agents also use specialized tools to find information online
They don’t type questions directly into the Google search bar; in fact, they often don’t even access the websites they reference
Instead, they query text databases collected by simple search crawler bots

People who want to make web content specifically for agents can take advantage of these crawlers: Time has pioneered that approach by serving its agent-oriented ads to crawlers in the hopes that they will be incorporated into these databases and surface when agents search for information

title: Not in a FEMA flood zone? Your home could still be at risk – and you could suffer more than your neighbor

<title>Not in a FEMA flood zone? Your home could still be at risk – and you could suffer more than your neighbor</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764630/original/file-20261007-50-jptlpb.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=313%2C269%2C4251%2C2834&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Floodwater from Hurricane Beryl affected Houston neighbors in different ways in July 2024.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/home-is-surrounded-in-floodwater-during-hurricane-beryl-on-news-photo/2161208691">Brandon Bell/Getty Images)</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem. No one requires you to buy flood insurance, and the map suggests you’re in the clear. But reality may be very different.</p>

<p><a href="https://firststreet.org/research-library/understanding-fema-flood-maps-and-limitations">Mounting evidence</a> reveals that significantly more homes are at risk of flooding than is indicated by FEMA’s 100-year flood maps – <a href="https://assets.firststreet.org/uploads/2020/06/first_street_foundation__first_national_flood_risk_assessment.pdf">about 6 million more</a>, and 14.6 million properties in all, by one estimate. The official maps are <a href="https://firststreet.org/research-library/understanding-fema-flood-maps-and-limitations">commonly outdated</a>, and <a href="https://kinder.rice.edu/urbanedge/new-fema-map-would-add-200-square-miles-115k-housing-units-harris-county-floodplains">some are two decades old</a>. Even when updated, they typically rely on historical flood data rather than future risk projections.</p>

<p>But there’s another problem that redrawing the lines won’t solve.</p>

<p>FEMA’s <a href="https://msc.fema.gov/portal/home">flood maps</a> answer only one question: Is the water likely to reach my neighborhood? They don’t assess an individual home’s risks or <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-if-texas-destructive-tax-day-storm-had-centered-on-inner-houston-instead-its-why-cities-should-plan-for-the-improbable-279964">what the impacts are likely to be</a> when the water rises. </p>

<p>To understand the impact, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apgeog.2026.104204">more comprehensive data is needed</a>, including the probable flood depth at the home, the building’s age and construction quality, and insurance coverage.</p>



<h2>Same street, different risks</h2>

<p>When these other factors are considered, your home’s true flood risk is far more complex than the map might seem to indicate.</p>

<p>The data shows how two houses on the same street can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apgeog.2026.104204">face radically different risks from flooding</a>, even when located in the same flood zone – and where local governments can help.</p>

<p>One home may be newer, well maintained and covered by flood insurance. Another may be decades older, at the low end of the same street where water runs deeper during a flood, and is in poor repair and uninsured. The same storm would leave them in very different predicaments, with very different paths to recovery.</p>

The background colors reflect the flood vulnerability index scores. Darker colors indicate higher risk.</span>

<p>Neighborhood averages can make it hard to tell which homes are likely to be hit hardest. But understanding an individual property’s risks matters for residents figuring out how to protect a home, and for local officials deciding where limited flood-protection money should go. </p>

<p>We <a href="https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1339-6473">study</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=QXQhGBwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">how flooding</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=vu9kFXEAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">affects homes</a> and the people who live in them. To see how much these house-by-house differences matter, we and colleagues Aaron Flores of Arizona State University and Sara Meerow of the University of Colorado Boulder built a detailed flood risk score for nearly 1 million homes in Houston. We describe the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apgeog.2026.104204">results in a new study</a> published in the journal Applied Geography.</p>

<p>Our past <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11111-025-00485-8">research in Houston</a> found that more than half of 100,000 documented flood-prone buildings in the city currently lie outside official flood boundaries, and that these overlooked buildings are more likely to be in poor condition and uninsured, leaving them especially exposed when the floodwaters do come. </p>

<p>The new research helps communities locate those homes.</p>

<h2>4 things that make a home vulnerable</h2>

<p>To get a better understanding of each household’s vulnerability, we combined <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apgeog.2026.104204">four types of information</a> about each home.</p>

<ul>
<li><strong>Water</strong>: How deep would floodwaters likely get at the home in a 100-year flood event, defined as having a 1% chance of occurrence in any given year? Here, we took a national flood model’s map of estimated parcel-level flood depths across Harris County and recorded the estimated depth at each residence.</li>
</ul>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

            </figcaption>

<ul>
<li><strong>Building</strong>: How old is the home, and how well has it been constructed and maintained? Older, lower-quality homes in poor repair <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11111-025-00485-8">tend to suffer more damage</a> when floodwater enters the structure. County appraisal records collected by expert assessors can provide critical pieces of information for making such judgments.</li>
</ul>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764015/original/file-20261005-50-vk2age.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A map of Houston shows building quality varying within neighborhoods." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764015/original/file-20261005-50-vk2age.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764015/original/file-20261005-50-vk2age.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=317&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764015/original/file-20261005-50-vk2age.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=317&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764015/original/file-20261005-50-vk2age.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=317&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764015/original/file-20261005-50-vk2age.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764015/original/file-20261005-50-vk2age.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764015/original/file-20261005-50-vk2age.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

              <span class="caption">A map of Houston shows how differences in building quality, based on the Harris Central Appraisal District’s assessments of the materials and workmanship used to construct each home, are mixed within neighborhoods.</span>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<ul>
<li><strong>Mobility</strong>: How busy are the roads nearby? For each home, we measured typical traffic within about a half-mile and within 3 miles. The busier those surrounding roads, the more a flood disrupts trips to work, school and hospitals, and the harder it is for first responders to get in and trapped residents to get out.</li>
</ul>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764656/original/file-20261007-60-5fwyou.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A map showing pockets with higher rates, often near lakes or rivers." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764656/original/file-20261007-60-5fwyou.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764656/original/file-20261007-60-5fwyou.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=312&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764656/original/file-20261007-60-5fwyou.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=312&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764656/original/file-20261007-60-5fwyou.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=312&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764656/original/file-20261007-60-5fwyou.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=392&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764656/original/file-20261007-60-5fwyou.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=392&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/764656/original/file-20261007-60-5fwyou.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=392&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<ul>
<li><strong>Finances</strong>: How much would it cost to repair the home, and what share of nearby homes have flood insurance? Neither keeps water out of a home, but both reflect what it costs to recover.</li>
</ul>

<p>We chose these four criteria because flood research consistently highlights their importance for how hard a flood hits a community: <a href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2020wr028673">how much water arrives</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11111-025-00485-8">how well the building holds up</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1061/%28ASCE%29NH.1527-6996.0000355">whether people can still get around</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10527001.2020.1840131">how big the repair bill is for the owner</a>. They aren’t the only possible measures; a city could use others within each category, depending on available data.</p>

<h2>What we found</h2>

<p>Homes in the same neighborhood can have very different flood vulnerability scores. In fact, we found the scores <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apgeog.2026.104204">differed more from house to house</a> within a neighborhood than from one neighborhood to the next.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Not every house in a neighborhood experiences flooding in the same way.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-an-aerial-view-flood-waters-inundate-a-neighborhood-on-news-photo/2157452645">Joe Raedle/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In practice, this means that knowing a neighborhood’s flood risk doesn’t necessarily tell you how hard a flood could hit any individual home. A neighborhood could look safe on average while <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/24694452.2022.2085656">containing some of the county’s riskiest homes</a>, and there may be many well-protected homes in an otherwise risky neighborhood. Much of the problem, we show, lies at the scale of buildings, not neighborhoods or ZIP codes.</p>

<h2>What residents and communities can do</h2>

<p>Homeowners can check several of these risks themselves. </p>

<p>Ask longtime neighbors or your city’s flood plain office whether your home or the street has been flooded before. Look up the home’s age in <a href="https://realestate.usnews.com/real-estate/articles/how-to-look-up-the-history-of-your-house">local property records</a> and have an inspector assess its condition. Find out whether the routes to work and school flood easily. And check whether you have a <a href="https://www.floodsmart.gov/">flood insurance policy</a>, and what it covers: Most homeowner’s policies don’t cover flood damage.</p>

<p>Communities can apply our approach with their own data to locate particularly vulnerable housing where neighborhood averages may disguise the need for help. They can start with existing address-level flood scores, such as <a href="https://firststreet.org/">First Street’s</a>, and add local records on buildings, roads and insurance. The extra details matter because officials have limited money for <a href="https://www.semswa.org/6-ways-to-flood-proof">flood-proofing homes</a>, <a href="https://cronin.engineer/foundation-drainage-secrets-for-a-safer-stronger-home/">improving drainage</a> and helping families recover after floods. Better data on buildings and flood risk can help them invest wisely.</p>

<p>Data similar to that used for Houston exists across much of the United States, so other flood-prone cities could follow the same approach.</p>

<p>Floods don’t stop at the lines on a map, and they don’t hit every house on a street the same. We believe it’s time for residents and local flood authorities to prepare accordingly.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293658/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Disaster aid has become a political lottery – libraries, schools and places of worship are stepping into the breach</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765998/original/file-20261013-50-blha8o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C7001%2C4667&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Volunteers assess tornado damage in Union City, Mich., on March 7, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=michigan%20tornado&amp;mediaType=photo">Nam Y. Huh/AP Photo</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Four tornadoes tore across southwest Michigan in early March 2026, killing four people. They were the state’s deadliest <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/detroit/news/whitmer-appeals-fema-denial-federal-aid-deadly-march-tornadoes/">natural hazards in decades</a>. </p>

<p>Gov. Gretchen Whitmer asked the Federal Emergency Management Agency for assistance to cover uninsured and underinsured losses. FEMA said no. She appealed. FEMA said <a href="https://wwmt.com/news/arc/fema-denies-michigan-appeal-tornado-damagee-branch-cass-stjoseph-counties-march-sixth-residents-rebuilding-homes-union-city-state-weather">no again</a>. </p>

<p>I study how communities prepare for and recover from disasters. As Dean’s Professor of Resilience at <a href="https://cssh.northeastern.edu/faculty/daniel-aldrich/">Northeastern University</a>, I have written six books on the topic, including the forthcoming “<a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/beyond-common-ground/paper">Beyond Common Ground</a>.” </p>

<p>The fact that Michigan was repeatedly denied aid reflects a broader shift, one that is putting more weight on the ties between neighbors and the places where they meet.</p>

<h2>Federal help is less predictable</h2>

<p>The Trump administration denied 26% of major disaster declarations in 2025, more than <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/administrations-arbitrary-unlawful-cuts-fema-funding-and-staff-threaten">double the rate of the year before</a> and well above the 15% denial average of the past two decades.</p>

<p>Denials have not fallen evenly. One study looked at some 2,500 disaster declarations since FEMA’s creation in 1979 in states where the governor and U.S. senators were all Republican or all Democrat. In his second term, Trump approved nearly 90% of requests from all-Republican states while approving only 23% of those from <a href="https://www.eenews.net/articles/its-three-times-harder-for-blue-states-to-get-disaster-funding-under-trump/">all-Democratic states</a>.</p>

<p>Colorado, an all-Democratic state, had both of its 2025 appeals for disaster rejected. They were Colorado’s <a href="https://www.kunc.org/news/2026-04-14/colorado-will-not-receive-fema-aid-for-last-years-fires-and-flooding">first denials since the 1980s</a>. </p>

<p>Florida, an all-Republican state, fared differently. In June, Trump announced 
US$416 million for the state’s disasters without specifying which one, adding that much of it would go to the <a href="https://www.wjhg.com/2026/07/01/florida-receives-4159-million-disaster-declaration-request/">Panhandle, one of his “favorite places</a>.” There, <a href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/weather/2026/01/25/winter-storm-snow-ice-storm-live-updates/88323930007/">a January 2025 snowstorm</a> was linked to 13 deaths and caused approximately $200 million in damages.</p>

<p>Nationally, an analysis of FEMA data by Andrew Rumbach, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute, found that about 84% of requests from states Trump won in 2024 were approved during his second term, <a href="https://andrewrumbach.com/fema.html">compared with about 42% from states he lost</a>.</p>

<p>While the White House has <a href="https://www.abc10.com/article/news/nation-world/trump-disaster-declarations-blue-states/507-5978fe83-84af-448b-99b9-8a0997bbe5ae">denied that politics plays a role</a> in who receives aid after shocks, local communities are now shouldering more of the cost of preparing for, responding to and recovering from disasters than they did before 2025. </p>

<p>FEMA owes local governments <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/04/10/nx-s1-5770433/delay-funding-fema-hurricanes-disasters-wildfires-floods">almost $10 billion in reimbursements</a> for recovery work that cities and towns have already paid for. When a declaration is denied, towns can be left covering costs as high as <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/administrations-arbitrary-unlawful-cuts-fema-funding-and-staff-threaten">15% of their annual budget</a>. <a href="https://www.philanthropy.com/news/as-fema-falters-philanthropy-is-forced-to-step-up/">Philanthropies</a> and aid groups such as Team Rubicon are expanding their roles to fill the gaps. </p>

<p>Nonprofits and community organizations cannot replace federal funding, but they can <a href="https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0002764214550299">build cooperation, trust and collective action</a>, which can better prepare neighborhoods and accelerate recovery.</p>

<h2>What connected places do</h2>

<p>In Union City, Michigan, help arrived within hours of the <a href="https://www.woodtv.com/news/branch-county/cleanup-continues-after-deadly-tornadoes-in-southwest-michigan/">EF3 tornado</a> that killed three people in March 2026. It came not from Washington but from neighbors. </p>

<p>School administrators turned the local <a href="https://www.detroitnews.com/story/weather/2026/03/08/union-city-school-tornado-volunteer-donations-help-village-branch-cass-storm-recovery/89055090007/">high school into a shelter</a> the night of the storm, volunteers arrived with food and supplies, and the local United Way opened a relief fund.</p>

<p>That is typical: Local residents are almost always the first responders after disasters strike. What was different is that federal help never followed.</p>

<p>Donations poured into the local high school, and the superintendent said <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/3-dead-12-injured-tornado-105025816.html">staff worked out how to get supplies to the people who needed them</a>. A local church, damaged in the storm, started a disaster fund to help residents <a href="https://www.wxyz.com/news/union-city-church-damaged-by-tornado-plans-to-help-fund-home-repairs">pay their insurance deductibles</a>.</p>

<p>Research on U.S. disasters shows how places such as schools, faith-based organizations and libraries can keep communities knit together.</p>

<p>After Hurricane Katrina in August 2005, floodwaters as high as 12 feet (3.6 meters) covered the low-income neighborhood around the Mary Queen of Vietnam Church in east New Orleans. Yet by summer 2007, about 90% of its residents had returned to their homes. For the city as a whole, <a href="https://www.mercatus.org/hayekprogram/research/journal-articles/club-goods-and-post-disaster-community-return">the figure hit only 45%</a>. The difference was likely the leadership of the Rev. Vien Nguyen, who coordinated supplies, organized volunteers and kept scattered residents in touch even as they evacuated to other states.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765999/original/file-20261013-50-1xnp02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man dressed in black with a white collar near his neck surveys a damaged room." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765999/original/file-20261013-50-1xnp02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765999/original/file-20261013-50-1xnp02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765999/original/file-20261013-50-1xnp02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765999/original/file-20261013-50-1xnp02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765999/original/file-20261013-50-1xnp02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765999/original/file-20261013-50-1xnp02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765999/original/file-20261013-50-1xnp02.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">In 2005, Bishop Dominic Loung returned home from Houston, Texas, to Mary Queen of Vietnam Church in New Orleans to survey damage from Hurricane Katrina.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/new-orleans-la-bishop-dominic-loung-of-the-diocese-of-news-photo/564050391?phrase=Mary%20Queen%20of%20Vietnam%20church%20in%20New%20Orleans%20East&amp;adppopup=true">Rick Loomis/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>My lab’s research during the COVID-19 pandemic found a similar pattern. We compared U.S. counties that were alike in many ways but differed in their social ties. After accounting for politics, governance, healthcare quality and demographics, our study found that <a href="http://doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2021.114241">two kinds of ties reduced the pandemic’s toll</a>: bonding ties and linking ties.</p>

<p>Bonding ties connect neighbors and family. </p>

<p>Linking ties connect residents to officials. Those ties are often built through spaces designed for connection, such as libraries and faith-based organizations like Nguyen’s church in New Orleans. </p>

<p>Libraries continue to safeguard our most vulnerable. In 2025, 44.7% of U.S. public libraries served as cooling or warming centers during extreme temperatures, <a href="https://www.ala.org/sites/default/files/2026-06/PLA_Services_Report_2026.pdf">up 8.2% from 2022</a>. </p>

<p>Many could do more. In a national survey, 84% of library directors agreed that libraries have a critical role in disaster response. Yet only 36% knew that federal law allows libraries to seek FEMA relocation funding to move to safer ground, and <a href="https://knowledge.uchicago.edu/records/rp2q6-54253">just 51% had an emergency preparedness plan</a>. </p>

<h2>A low-cost layer of protection</h2>

<p>In my <a href="https://www.ucpress.edu/books/beyond-common-ground/paper">new book</a>, I show that more than 90% of federal disaster funds went to roads, utilities and other standard infrastructure in the early 21st century, and less than 10% to libraries, parks, schools, places of worship and community centers, where neighbors check on one another and organize recovery. </p>

<p>Federal aid may go to rebuild some of these spaces, but it rarely pays to keep them open and running when communities need them most.</p>

<p>In another study, I found that Japanese communities with higher density of social infrastructure had half the number of deaths from a catastrophic tsunami in March 2011 compared to <a href="http://doi.org/10.1017/S1468109922000366">similar communities with fewer gathering spaces</a>. </p>

<p>In my assessment, as federal aid becomes less predictable, these kinds of places people frequent often will have to carry us into the future. The communities that recover best from the next disaster may be the ones that kept their libraries open, their civic halls full of volunteers and their parks full of residents.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292948/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
