<title>Students who attended Miami-Dade public school pre-K outperformed peers in 18-year study</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/768610/original/file-20261027-52-efy8le.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=135%2C0%2C6663%2C4441&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Research shows high-quality preschool benefits kids later.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/kindergarten-music-class-royalty-free-image/2164665292?phrase=miami-dade%20preschool%20hispanic&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">FatCamera/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Choosing a preschool is a difficult and important decision. Parents are weighing cost, proximity and convenience with how each program meets the needs of the child and matches the goals and values of their family and cultural community.</p>

<p>This choice makes a difference. Research in early education clearly shows that children who attend high-quality preschool programs – those with smaller class sizes, a developmentally appropriate curriculum, warm teacher-child interactions and established, efficient routines – are <a href="https://www.fcd-us.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/Evidence-Base-on-Preschool-Education-FINAL.pdf">better prepared for kindergarten</a>.</p>

<p>We are <a href="https://case.fiu.edu/about/directory/profiles/bleiker-charles.html">researchers</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=_Ekthu4AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">who study</a> <a href="https://www.linkedin.com/in/kaitlynmumma/">early childhood education</a>, and we conducted an 18-year study <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2026.03.004">tracking the academic progress</a> of 27,814 students who attended different types of prekindergarten in Miami and then went on to attend the Miami-Dade County Public Schools system from kindergarten through high school. We found that the type of pre-K program the children attended made a difference for their overall educational outcomes.</p>

<h2>How we did our study</h2>

<p>From 2002 to 2007, we partnered with Miami-Dade County Public Schools, early childcare providers across the county and the <a href="https://www.elcmdm.org/">Early Learning Coalition of Miami-Dade</a>, a nonprofit that works with childcare providers and communities to promote school readiness, with the goal of assessing five cohorts of about 10,000 students per year.</p>

<p>School readiness takes into consideration the children’s cognitive, language, motor and social skills, as well as behavior problems. During the study, we shared the data we collected with parents, teachers and center directors to inform interventions for struggling kids and improvements to their pre-K programs.</p>

<p>Some of the students in these five cohorts attended taxpayer-funded, public school pre-K programs, while some received federal subsidies administered through the state of Florida to attend center-based or family childcare at age 4.</p>

<p>Center-based programs, like a Kiddie Academy, for example, can be nonprofit or for-profit centers in the community. They operate either in a freestanding location or as part of a corporate or faith-based building. Family or home-based childcare programs are generally smaller and operate out of private residences.</p>

<p>After the children had moved through pre-K, we continued to receive their anonymized academic records each year, as long as they stayed in the public school system. The last cohort of students completed 12th grade in spring 2020.</p>

<h2>Outcomes in later grades</h2>

<p>We found that children who attended public school pre-K programs at age 4 <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2026.03.004">achieved the strongest third-grade outcomes</a> on standardized reading and math test scores and GPA. These children outperformed those who attended center-based care, who in turn generally performed better than children who were enrolled in family childcare. Kids who attended public school pre-K were 35% less likely to be held back in third grade compared with the other groups.</p>

<p>Further, we found that kids who attended higher-quality elementary schools – as <a href="https://www.fldoe.org/accountability/accountability-reporting/school-grades/">measured by the Florida Department of Education</a> – did better on average.</p>

<p>However, the quality of the elementary school that students went on to attend didn’t change the differences we observed across the early childhood education types, except when it came to reading skills. Students who attended center-based care and went on to attend higher-quality schools were better able to catch up to the public school pre-K kids by third grade in reading.</p>

<p>Our findings are consistent with most previous studies of public pre-K. Students who attended public pre-K <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13308">programs in Boston</a>; <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/pam.22023">Tulsa, Oklahoma</a>; and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12645">North Carolina</a> have shown better results on standardized test scores, lower absenteeism and better grade retention when compared with children who attended other programs, even as late as eighth grade.</p>

<p>However, there are outliers. Children who attended the publicly funded voluntary pre-K program in Tennessee did not perform any better than other children on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2018.03.005">third</a> or <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001301">sixth grade outcomes</a> – and in some cases, they performed worse.</p>

<p>Previous findings are also mixed on whether these effects <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100620915848">persist past the third grade</a>.</p>

<p>In our study, it appears that the long-term benefits of public school pre-K extend through eighth grade, but this conclusion is still in peer review and has not been published yet. We are currently examining whether benefits persist throughout high school.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766264/original/file-20261014-50-m9maov.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="woman talking to children at a table with blocks" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766264/original/file-20261014-50-m9maov.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766264/original/file-20261014-50-m9maov.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766264/original/file-20261014-50-m9maov.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766264/original/file-20261014-50-m9maov.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766264/original/file-20261014-50-m9maov.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766264/original/file-20261014-50-m9maov.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766264/original/file-20261014-50-m9maov.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Teachers who have been educated in working with young children can have a measurable effect on a child’s future academic success.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/female-teacher-helping-little-boy-sort-the-cubes-by-royalty-free-image/1493162902?phrase=preschool%20classroom&amp;adppopup=true">Vadym Buinov/Moment via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Collective resources</h2>

<p>Why did kids in public school pre-K programs do better compared to center-based and family childcare? We believe that the answer likely lies in the quality and organizational differences between the three different types of early care and education.</p>

<p>The public school pre-K programs in our study benefited from the collective resources of the fourth-largest public school system in the country. This matters for everything from the quality of teachers they are able to hire to the facilities and curriculum.</p>

<p>Miami-Dade public schools require teachers to have at minimum a bachelor’s degree and a teaching credential, whereas the others required less education at the time of our study. Public pre-K teachers’ certification allows them to teach from pre-K to third grade, so they typically bring their experience of teaching in kindergarten and the early elementary grades to the pre-K classroom.</p>

<p>These programs also used a developmentally appropriate curriculum, while the others used a variety of materials and approaches. When we began this study, the center-based programs were mostly independent, unaffiliated sites, although some for-profits had more than one center in the study, and some nonprofit organizations such as Catholic Charities or the YMCA oversaw multiple centers.</p>

<p>Many of the children in the study moved from one school to another within the same district. Because Miami-Dade’s public schools are part of a countywide system, the children’s academic records moved with them easily, so their new teacher could see their progress. And since the curriculum was the same across the district, the students were able to pick up at their new school where they’d left off.</p>

<p>This continuity could also explain why children who entered the public school system in pre-K performed better than those outside it. The majority of the children in the study went on to attend public elementary school. The kids in public school preschool and their parents were therefore already familiar with the schools that they would be attending the following year. It’s not hard to see how this would be an advantage for a child transitioning from preschool to kindergarten.</p>

<h2>Better than ever</h2>

<p>Our findings do not indicate to us, however, that every child must attend public school pre-K in order to succeed in school later on. The reality in Miami-Dade County – and in most communities – is that we need all forms of early care and education, and each setting serves important needs for families.</p>

<p>Indeed, students in all three types of programs made excellent school readiness gains from the beginning to the end of the age-4 academic year. It was just that the children in the public school preschools made stronger gains.</p>

<p>Center- and home-based care in Miami-Dade County is much higher quality across the board today than when we began our study back in 2002. Many more centers are accredited, and teacher education levels have improved. In fact, in our assessment, the quality of early education in Miami-Dade County <a href="https://www.elcmdm.org/article/3043765">has never been better</a>.</p>

<p>Still, the cohesive system offered by public schools remains the gold standard for preschool when serving most children and families. In terms of teacher preparation and qualifications, standardized curriculum, oversight and alignment with the kindergarten curriculum, public school pre-k for low-income families in Miami still offers the best hope of long-term academic success.</p>

body: Research shows high-quality preschool benefits kids later
FatCamera/E+ via Getty Images Choosing a preschool is a difficult and important decision
Parents are weighing cost, proximity and convenience with how each program meets the needs of the child and matches the goals and values of their family and cultural community

Research in early education clearly shows that children who attend high-quality preschool programs – those with smaller class sizes, a developmentally appropriate curriculum, warm teacher-child interactions and established, efficient routines – are better prepared for kindergarten

We are researchers who study early childhood education , and we conducted an 18-year study tracking the academic progress of 27,814 students who attended different types of prekindergarten in Miami and then went on to attend the Miami-Dade County Public Schools system from kindergarten through high school
We found that the type of pre-K program the children attended made a difference for their overall educational outcomes

How we did our study From 2002 to 2007, we partnered with Miami-Dade County Public Schools, early childcare providers across the county and the Early Learning Coalition of Miami-Dade , a nonprofit that works with childcare providers and communities to promote school readiness, with the goal of assessing five cohorts of about 10,000 students per year
School readiness takes into consideration the children’s cognitive, language, motor and social skills, as well as behavior problems
During the study, we shared the data we collected with parents, teachers and center directors to inform interventions for struggling kids and improvements to their pre-K programs

Some of the students in these five cohorts attended taxpayer-funded, public school pre-K programs, while some received federal subsidies administered through the state of Florida to attend center-based or family childcare at age 4
Center-based programs, like a Kiddie Academy, for example, can be nonprofit or for-profit centers in the community
They operate either in a freestanding location or as part of a corporate or faith-based building
Family or home-based childcare programs are generally smaller and operate out of private residences
After the children had moved through pre-K, we continued to receive their anonymized academic records each year, as long as they stayed in the public school system
The last cohort of students completed 12th grade in spring 2020
Outcomes in later grades We found that children who attended public school pre-K programs at age 4 achieved the strongest third-grade outcomes on standardized reading and math test scores and GPA
These children outperformed those who attended center-based care, who in turn generally performed better than children who were enrolled in family childcare
Kids who attended public school pre-K were 35% less likely to be held back in third grade compared with the other groups
Further, we found that kids who attended higher-quality elementary schools – as measured by the Florida Department of Education – did better on average

However, the quality of the elementary school that students went on to attend didn’t change the differences we observed across the early childhood education types, except when it came to reading skills
Students who attended center-based care and went on to attend higher-quality schools were better able to catch up to the public school pre-K kids by third grade in reading
Our findings are consistent with most previous studies of public pre-K

Students who attended public pre-K programs in Boston ; Tulsa, Oklahoma ; and North Carolina have shown better results on standardized test scores, lower absenteeism and better grade retention when compared with children who attended other programs, even as late as eighth grade

Children who attended the publicly funded voluntary pre-K program in Tennessee did not perform any better than other children on third or sixth grade outcomes – and in some cases, they performed worse
Previous findings are also mixed on whether these effects persist past the third grade
In our study, it appears that the long-term benefits of public school pre-K extend through eighth grade, but this conclusion is still in peer review and has not been published yet
We are currently examining whether benefits persist throughout high school
Teachers who have been educated in working with young children can have a measurable effect on a child’s future academic success

Vadym Buinov/Moment via Getty Images Collective resources Why did kids in public school pre-K programs do better compared to center-based and family childcare? We believe that the answer likely lies in the quality and organizational differences between the three different types of early care and education
The public school pre-K programs in our study benefited from the collective resources of the fourth-largest public school system in the country
This matters for everything from the quality of teachers they are able to hire to the facilities and curriculum
Miami-Dade public schools require teachers to have at minimum a bachelor’s degree and a teaching credential, whereas the others required less education at the time of our study

Public pre-K teachers’ certification allows them to teach from pre-K to third grade, so they typically bring their experience of teaching in kindergarten and the early elementary grades to the pre-K classroom
These programs also used a developmentally appropriate curriculum, while the others used a variety of materials and approaches

When we began this study, the center-based programs were mostly independent, unaffiliated sites, although some for-profits had more than one center in the study, and some nonprofit organizations such as Catholic Charities or the YMCA oversaw multiple centers
Many of the children in the study moved from one school to another within the same district
Because Miami-Dade’s public schools are part of a countywide system, the children’s academic records moved with them easily, so their new teacher could see their progress
And since the curriculum was the same across the district, the students were able to pick up at their new school where they’d left off
This continuity could also explain why children who entered the public school system in pre-K performed better than those outside it
The majority of the children in the study went on to attend public elementary school

<title>Getting a big head start on holiday shopping can benefit retailers and consumers alike</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769285/original/file-20261030-64-w44w5o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C2800%2C1866&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Does it make sense to wait until late December to wrap up, like these California shoppers did in 2023?</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/maya-bryant-of-los-angeles-makes-her-way-with-shopping-bags-news-photo/1870881445?adppopup=true">Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Amazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales <a href="https://www.wkbw.com/life/money/interactive-holiday-deals-started-early-heres-where-shopping-now-pays-off">as early as October</a>.</p>

<p>But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping.</p>

<p>As a finance professor <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=rfH2gbQAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">who studies how people and companies make financial decisions</a>, I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping.</p>



<h2>Why retailers get such an early start</h2>

<p>Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about <a href="https://nrf.com/research-insights/holiday-data-and-trends/winter-holidays">US$1 trillion</a> to <a href="https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/about/press-room/deloitte-forecasts-holiday-retail-sales.html">$1.7 trillion</a> in the U.S.</p>

<p>Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the <a href="https://newsroom.bankofamerica.com/content/newsroom/press-releases/2026/10/bank-of-america-study--early-december-could-overtake-black-frida.html">Bank of America Holiday Spending survey</a>.</p>

<p>But many people like to <a href="https://www.cnet.com/tech/holiday-shopping-2026/">shop for holiday gifts</a> early – <a href="https://nrf.com/research-insights/holiday-data-and-trends/winter-holidays">meaning before Halloween</a>. Some do this <a href="https://massmarketretailers.com/holiday-shoppers-focus-on-deals-as-economic-concerns-shape-spending/">out of necessity</a>: They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks. </p>

<p>For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of <a href="https://nrf.com/media-center/press-releases/consumers-to-spend-second-highest-amount-on-record-according-to-nrf-holiday-survey">early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually</a>. In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping.</p>

<p>Retailers are adjusting by getting an <a href="https://www.gourmetgiftbaskets.com/Blog/post/how-early-do-americans-start-holiday-shopping.aspx">early start on holiday sales</a> and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more <a href="https://www.investing.com/news/economic-indicators/us-holiday-sales-growth-to-speed-up-as-shoppers-stay-resilientnrf-forecasts-4952241">people to join the early birds</a>. </p>

<p>And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season. </p>

<p>A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may <a href="https://www.modernretail.co/operations/a-shorter-shopping-window-complicates-retails-already-challenging-holiday-season/">ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics</a>, since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs.</p>

<p>Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory <a href="https://ecommfs.com/seasonal-inventory-planning-month-by-month-guide/">gives retailers more opportunities to sell</a> those items. However, an earlier shopping season does <a href="https://www.nmrk.com/insights/thought-leadership/holiday-shopping-2026-an-earlier-start-a-longer-season-and-its-effects-on-u-s-retail-real-estate">not necessarily increase consumer spending</a> overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769287/original/file-20261030-64-zyynxy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Holiday decorations line a store's full shelves." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769287/original/file-20261030-64-zyynxy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769287/original/file-20261030-64-zyynxy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769287/original/file-20261030-64-zyynxy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769287/original/file-20261030-64-zyynxy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769287/original/file-20261030-64-zyynxy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769287/original/file-20261030-64-zyynxy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769287/original/file-20261030-64-zyynxy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Early birds could buy these Christmas decorations at a discount on Oct. 17, 2026.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/christmas-decorations-for-sale-in-a-retail-store-pleasant-news-photo/2301017101?adppopup=true">Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Beware of some early-shopping pitfalls</h2>

<p>To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/shelleykohan/2022/10/30/consumers-say-hassle-free-returns-are-more-important-than-ever/">read vendors’ fine print</a> and <a href="https://www.bbb.org/holiday/shopping/holiday-returns-and-exchanges">research their return policies</a>.</p>

<p>Many big retailers are <a href="https://www.loopreturns.com/blog/setting-up-the-right-holiday-returns-policy/">making their return policies more restrictive</a> by <a href="https://idahobusinessreview.com/2025/11/19/retailers-tighten-return-policies-holiday-shopping/">shortening the length of time you can return purchases</a> and adding return/restocking fees. </p>

<p>In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, <a href="https://www.bestbuy.com/site/help-topics/return-exchange-policy/pcmcat260800050014.c?id=pcmcat260800050014">Best Buy’s extended policy</a> takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. <a href="https://www.target.com/help/article/000061980">Target similarly restricts</a> its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.valueaddedresource.net/amazon-2026-holiday-returns/">Amazon extended its holiday return</a> policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769288/original/file-20261030-64-i3rxmp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman shops online on her laptop with a Christmas tree in the background." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769288/original/file-20261030-64-i3rxmp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769288/original/file-20261030-64-i3rxmp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769288/original/file-20261030-64-i3rxmp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769288/original/file-20261030-64-i3rxmp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769288/original/file-20261030-64-i3rxmp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769288/original/file-20261030-64-i3rxmp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769288/original/file-20261030-64-i3rxmp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The timing of holiday shopping varies whether you buy gifts online or in brick-and-mortar stores.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/woman-buying-christmas-gift-on-her-laptop-royalty-free-image/2182687505?adppopup=true">Anchiy/E+ via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>When buying early makes financial sense</h2>

<p>Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary. </p>

<p>For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price.</p>

<p>But that doesn’t mean <a href="https://www.consumeraffairs.com/news/the-hidden-danger-of-shopping-for-christmas-too-early-the-one-more-gift-trap-102926.html">you necessarily need to rush</a> to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out. </p>

<p>And you should do some <a href="https://lookfor.ai/blog/what-is-the-purpose-of-comparison-shopping">comparison shopping</a> to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items.</p>

<p>Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The <a href="https://www.pnfp.com/learning-center/personal-finance/managing-your-money/5-budgeting-tips-for-smart-holiday-shopping/">key is to have a budget</a>, recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294545/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Why do galaxies rotate?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766259/original/file-20261014-50-eorw8d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C177%2C2948%2C1965&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The spiral galaxy Messier 77. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://esahubble.org/news/heic1305/">NASA, ESA &amp; A. van der Hoeven</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nd/4.0/">CC BY-ND</a></span></figcaption></figure>

<p><em><a href="https://theconversation.com/topics/curious-kids-us-74795">Curious Kids</a> is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to <a href="mailto:curiouskidsus@theconversation.com">CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com</a>.</em></p>

<hr>

<blockquote>
<p><strong>Why do galaxies spin or rotate? 
– Swara Dhat, age 13, Thane, India</strong></p>
</blockquote>

<hr>

<p>Spinning is fun, and you can find many ways to do it. From carousels to an office chair, spinning is everywhere – even in outer space.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.rit.edu/science/experimental-cosmology-astrophysics">As astrophysicists</a>, we know that spinning – or rotating – is <a href="https://www.sciencefocus.com/space/why-everything-spins">extremely common in space</a>. The Earth, the Moon, the Sun, the entire Milky Way, and many things inside and outside of it, rotate. </p>

<p>But why is that? Why does anything rotate at all in space? To answer this question, we first need to understand how objects spin.</p>

<h2>Spinning has laws, too</h2>

<p>The amount of spin that an object has is called its <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/science/angular-momentum/">angular momentum</a>. It depends on the mass of the object and how that mass is distributed around the object’s <a href="https://biomechanist.net/center-of-mass/">center of mass</a>. <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Center_of_mass">The center of mass</a> is the location at which an object could be balanced on a point. Have you tried to balance a ruler on your finger? You balance it in the middle, which is the center of mass.</p>

<p>If something is spinning, and its mass and shape stay the same, its spinning speed stays the same. If its mass or the shape changes, its spinning speed also changes. Outside forces can change an object’s total amount of spin. </p>

<p>Think about spinning on a chair. If you first try spinning with your legs splayed out, you’ll find that you can pull your legs in to spin faster. This phenomenon is explained by <a href="https://openbooks.lib.msu.edu/collegephysics1/chapter/angular-momentum-and-its-conservation-2/">the law of conservation of angular momentum</a>. Pulling your legs inward changes your shape, and brings mass – your legs – closer to your center of mass, making you spin faster. Later, the chair slows down and stops. Its spinning parts rub against each other and <a href="https://www.sciencetimes.com/articles/62716/20261009/why-does-friction-produce-heat-understanding-physics-moving-objects.htm">warm up due to friction</a>, which converts moving energy into heat.</p>

<p>Another example is <a href="https://theconversation.com/from-ski-jumping-to-speedskating-winter-sports-represent-physics-in-action-272958">spinning figure skaters</a>, who spin faster when they pull their arms in. The law of conservation of angular momentum applies to everything, which means it applies to galaxies.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/FmnkQ2ytlO8?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Angular momentum allows figure skaters to speed up while spinning.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>How to build a galaxy</h2>

<p>Now that we understand how objects spin, let’s look at how galaxies form and why they spin.</p>

<p>Galaxies are extremely massive. They’re made up of regular matter, including stars, planets, gas, dust and people. They also contain <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/dark-matter/">dark matter</a>, which scientists know less about but can study through its gravitational pull on objects. </p>

<p>Both types of matter have mass: They can pull on each other through gravity, the same way Earth’s gravity keeps you anchored to the ground. When the universe first formed, <a href="https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/March18/Wechsler/frames.html">dark matter helped pull together</a> clouds of gas and dust to make galaxies. Imagine two clouds of gas and dust in space traveling toward each other from any direction. It would be unlikely for the clouds to collide perfectly head-on; more often, they approach off-center.  </p>

<p>The clouds share a center of mass, and depending on their relative speed, direction and mass, gravity may cause the clouds to spin into each other and fuse. As such, if the clouds manage to pull on each other and spiral into one another, the initial spiraling motion is conserved into the final rotation of the merged cloud, under the law of conservation of angular momentum.</p>

            <figcaption><span class="caption">This simulation shows how a galaxy, similar to our Milky Way, forms.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<figure>

            <figcaption><span class="caption">This video from NASA shows magnetic marbles thrown at each other in space. Pretend the marbles are the clouds. Sometimes, the marbles spin into each other and stick. Other times, the marbles miss each other. In every case, there is a total amount of spin that the marbles share, even if you cannot tell by eye.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Once the clouds spiral into each other, the material inside them collides. This collision squishes the clouds, changing their overall motion and <a href="https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/cloud-cloud-collision-ccc">heating them up</a> to the point of glowing. The clouds slow down as they pass through each other and move away, but they can no longer escape each other’s gravitational pull. They continue this spiral dance until they fuse into a larger rotating cloud. The process then repeats for bigger rotating clouds. </p>

<p>Depending on the angle, speed and mass of the clouds when they meet, these collisions can speed up, slow down or reverse the spinning. Eventually, the cloud becomes large enough that more collisions with smaller clouds do not affect the overall spinning motion by much.</p>

<p>Gas and dust also fall directly into the clouds, along with streams of matter called cosmic filaments. Together, <a href="https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/galaxies-fed-by-funnels-of-fuel/">clouds and filaments join</a> to form a rotating galaxy. This galaxy will continue to spin, unless something happens to it, such as merging with another galaxy.</p>

            <figcaption><span class="caption">This simulation, from the Royal Astronomical Society, shows the formation of a large galaxy.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The big three</h2>

<p>There are <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/science/universe-uncovered/hubble-galaxies/">three main</a> <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/universe/galaxies/types/#intro">types of galaxies</a>, each with different levels of organized spinning inside them.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.thoughtco.com/irregular-galaxies-mysteries-of-the-universe-3072046">Irregular galaxies</a> are blobs of gas, dust and stars. They have a general direction of rotation, though some objects do not follow it. </p>



<p><a href="https://esahubble.org/wordbank/spiral-galaxy/">Spiral galaxies</a> are more organized. They have a flat disk containing spiral arms, and a central galactic bulge. Most of the matter in the disk follows the same rotation direction, while things get a little messier in the center. The <a href="https://science.nasa.gov/missions/hubble/hubble-comes-face-to-face-with-spirals-arms/">spiral arms are like traffic jams</a> where there are more stars, gas and dust, and it takes matter more time to leave the spiral arms and enter the space between them.</p>



<p><a href="https://esahubble.org/wordbank/elliptical-galaxy/">Elliptical galaxies</a> have a lot of stars but very little gas and dust, and many are the result of galaxies merging together. The stars orbit the galactic center, but may or may not follow an organized rotation depending on its formation and merger history. </p>



<p>All galaxies spin, but not all galaxies spin the same way!</p>

<title>How to prepare your online life for your death</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769160/original/file-20261029-78-p4z95o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8660%2C5773&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">That list of passwords isn&#39;t enough to ensure your heirs can get into your online accounts.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/senior-woman-reading-letter-while-sitting-with-royalty-free-image/1340975092">Westend61 via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>What happens to all of your online accounts – credit cards, merchants, news subscriptions, social media, streaming services – after you die? How will your heirs know how to access these accounts or understand what you want done with them? Most people haven’t considered these questions, and this lack of planning can create significant headaches for next of kin. </p>

<p>We <a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791633">studied challenges older adults encounter</a> when thinking about what should happen to their online accounts after they die. We interviewed 21 American adults over age 60 to learn about their concerns, needs and practices for their online accounts, as well as what would make planning for these accounts easier.</p>

<p>Most of the people we interviewed had hired lawyers or estate planners to draft wills specifying how their money and physical property should be handled after their deaths. They wanted to make sure that heirs had easy access to the money and assets left behind. </p>

<p>People also wanted their relatives to have easy access to their digital estates, but they had not done any formal planning and didn’t know how to plan for transitioning or shutting down online accounts, such as email, social media and accounts for online bills. Some told us they hadn’t thought about their online accounts at all. Others said they assumed heirs would know what to do, or they assumed that giving heirs the passwords to accounts would be enough to grant access to their digital estates. </p>

<p>Unfortunately, more planning is typically necessary to smoothly transition a digital estate.</p>

<h2>Passing down a list of passwords</h2>

<p>The older adults we interviewed mainly kept track of their passwords by hand: They wrote their passwords down on paper, or they stored them in a digital file. Almost everyone had already shared some of their passwords with family members who help them manage their accounts. Everyone also believed that their heirs would be able to find their list of passwords after their death.</p>

<p>The people we interviewed weren’t always happy with their current systems for keeping track of their passwords. Some people complained that when accounts required frequent password changes, it was <a href="https://www.usenix.org/system/files/soups2019-pearman.pdf">difficult to keep their password lists up to date</a>. As a result, they weren’t sure their heirs would get the latest version of all their passwords.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.pcmag.com/picks/the-best-password-managers">Password managers</a> can be a good way to make sure passwords are up to date and, if set up appropriately, accessible to a designated heir. While most of the people we interviewed used password managers, some said they didn’t save important passwords in them because <a href="https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec21summer_ray.pdf">they didn’t know whether they were secure</a>. However, using a password manager is the <a href="https://www.usenix.org/conference/soups2025/presentation/ortloff">most frequent security recommendation from experts</a>, who typically use them to store passwords for all of their accounts. </p>

<p>By using a password manager, you can make sure your designated heir has access to all your latest passwords. Some password managers provide access for survivors by default, such as through <a href="https://support.nordpass.com/hc/en-us/articles/5691777958929-How-to-give-Emergency-Access-in-NordPass">time-delayed</a> <a href="https://bitwarden.com/help/emergency-access/">emergency access features</a>. You can also write the master password down somewhere safe to pass to your heir. Instead of making sure dozens of account passwords are up to date, you only have to manage one.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769165/original/file-20261029-64-v3kivk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="a middle aged man and woman sit at a table as a younger man stands between them, all looking at a laptop screen" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769165/original/file-20261029-64-v3kivk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/769165/original/file-20261029-64-v3kivk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769165/original/file-20261029-64-v3kivk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769165/original/file-20261029-64-v3kivk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769165/original/file-20261029-64-v3kivk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769165/original/file-20261029-64-v3kivk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/769165/original/file-20261029-64-v3kivk.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Your heirs could have a frustrating time accessing your online accounts even if they have your passwords.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/family-talking-and-doing-home-finances-on-laptop-at-royalty-free-image/2163890003">FG Trade Latin/E+ via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Passwords alone cannot unlock all accounts</h2>

<p>Unfortunately, just handing someone your passwords doesn’t always mean they can log in and manage your account. If the account asks for two-factor authentication, such as through a code sent to a phone or email, a password alone won’t grant access. And if the email account is closed or the phone number is no longer active after you die, then <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2024/02/26/tech/digital-legacy-planning-personal-technology/index.html">they might be out of luck</a>.</p>

<p>To make sure your heirs aren’t locked out, identify the devices and accounts that can act as keys for heirs to unlock the rest of your online accounts, and direct your heirs to keep them open until other accounts have been settled. This not only makes sure that heirs can get authentication codes, but also lets heirs reset passwords to your other accounts if they can’t find the password.</p>

<p>In some cases, passwords might not be necessary. Some online services, such as <a href="https://www.facebook.com/help/103897939701143/">Facebook</a> and <a href="https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/3036546?ai1hc=1">Google</a>, have features that let you choose someone to manage your account or get your data after you die. However, not all platforms offer this option, and few of the older adults we interviewed were aware of these features. </p>

<h2>Online accounts don’t automatically die with you</h2>

<p>Like many of the people we interviewed, you might also assume that heirs will properly deal with accounts with money and important data, while unimportant accounts can be ignored. But even if there is nothing important in an account, it can still be <a href="https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/safety-security/updating-our-inactive-account-policies/">used by hackers for identity theft, spam or fraudulent activities</a>. Automatic monthly charges, to cover the cost of streaming services or annual billing for magazine subscriptions, for example, might also continue for a long time.</p>

<p>Without instructions, the people managing your online accounts after you die might not think to close those accounts. They might also find it hard to guess your intentions.</p>

<p>You can leave instructions for your heirs by going through your accounts and noting which ones can be closed outright, which ones require final payments before closure, and which ones might require other actions. You can also periodically tidy up and close accounts you are no longer using to keep your list of accounts more manageable.</p>

<h2>Planning ahead for you and your heirs</h2>

<p>While it seems simple to just let your heirs handle your important online accounts and let the others slowly fade into nonexistence after you die, the reality is often more complex.</p>

<p>Your online accounts will live on after you die. Planning ahead for what happens to those accounts can reduce the stress on your heirs and ensure your digital accounts are handled according to your wishes.</p>

Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is closing out the midterms by talking about anything but.  What’s happening? If polls bear out, Republicans are a day away from a catastrophically bad midterms result, potentially losing control of both chambers of Congress.  Trump, however, has other things on his mind

On Monday, he made his final midterms pitch in a nearly hour-long press conference with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, where he focused heavily on the state of the newly reopened Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and his other DC construction projects (both planned and underway). “This is a massive piece of pool,” he said. “And it was treated with a lot of love and then it was treated with a lot of hate, and we’re going to stop the hate.”  What else has Trump been saying? Monday marked the culmination of the president’s strange campaign season, which has been heavy on disjointed rambling and musings about the posterior aspect of incumbent Republican Sen

Trump has also spent the past few months urging Americans to vote in the midterms as if he were on the ballot — but polling suggests he may be more of a drag than a boon to Republican candidates locked in close races.  What’s the big picture? We won’t know for sure how the midterms will turn out until polls close Tuesday night (and maybe not for a while after that, depending on how some key races turn out).  Trump, though, briefly acknowledged on Monday that things are looking bleak for his party: “For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms,” he said, “but we gave this a very strong shot.” And with that, it’s time to log off… This is a few days late in coming, but I’d be remiss if I didn’t share my colleague Ian Millhiser’s tribute to the late Patrick Stewart and his iconic role on Star Trek as  Captain Jean-Luc Picard
