title: What the polls can’t tell us about the midterms
excerpt: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. | Salwan Georges/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that he
body: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. | Salwan Georges/Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

We’re at T-minus eight hours until Election Day — at least here on the East Coast — and Democrats are likely feeling good about their electoral odds right now.  The party is strongly favored to win the House and make big gains in the Senate, with a serious chance of retaking both chambers
The final New York Times/Siena polls , released Sunday, put Democrats ahead of Republicans in at least five of the seven battleground states that will determine who holds the Senate
That includes Kansas and Texas, two states that haven’t elected a Democratic senator in generations
The picture appears so dim for Republicans that even President Donald Trump seemed to acknowledge it during remarks this afternoon: “For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms
We gave this a very strong shot.” But while many, many polls and pundits are forecasting a blue wave…I’m a little more cautious about making definitive predictions
Polling has only grown more difficult in recent years, as we saw especially clearly in the 2016 and 2020 elections

Go a little deeper View Link Polling methodology sounds complex. (And it is!) But one of the field’s biggest challenges is actually pretty easy to grasp: Some people enjoy chatting with pollsters and filling out little surveys on their phones…and some people could not care less
The poll-takers tend to be older, more educated, and more invested in politics
The poll-avoiders are often younger, less educated, and — in recent presidential contests — more likely to support Trump

Pollsters are aware of these imbalances and try to correct them by applying statistical adjustments after the fact, but it’s not a perfect science.  It’s difficult to gauge , for instance, how the Republicans who do respond to polls might differ from the ones who don’t
And it’s impossible to know for certain how many people who say they’re going to vote will actually drag themselves to their nearest school gymnasium or fire hall tomorrow
There are a few new wrinkles this year, too
Pollsters conducted fewer late-cycle surveys than they do in the typical midterm cycle, according to the Washington Post
That not only means that we have less data overall, but that the data we do have may not account for late-breaking developments, such as Democratic Rep

Haley Stevens’s surprise endorsement of a Republican in the Michigan Senate race or a ballot-stacking scandal in Alaska.  Several close Senate contests are also in rural states — think Alaska, Maine, and Iowa — where reaching a representative mix of voters can be especially difficult for pollsters
But even if the polls are right and a blue wave is likely, that doesn’t mean it will actually come to pass

My colleague Astead Herndon sees another possibility: The fear of a liberal takeover could motivate large numbers of Republicans to vote , even if they’ve soured on Trump or had previously planned to sit out this election.  None of this is to say that the blue wave won’t happen, to be clear, or that it won’t happen on the scale that some pundits have predicted
Polls just aren’t the same thing as elections.  One link for later ➨ Brace for political fights with your family
They are, after all, an election-year tradition! Instead of clapping back at relatives with different politics, try to get curious about their positions
If in doubt, deploy the line “why does that matter to you?” Then explain your own views with an “I” statement, rather than a put-down or accusation

Before you go… Did you know …that we’ve unwittingly dosed the world’s fish with anti-anxiety meds? Our bodies don’t entirely absorb these drugs, so trace amounts end up in our urine…and from there, in rivers and coastal habitats
Today’s trivia: Which US pharmaceutical giant was founded by a Union army veteran after the Civil War? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the name of the reclusive neighbor in Harper Lee’s classic novel To Kill a Mockingbird
That would be Arthur “Boo” Radley, played by Robert Duvall in the 1962 film adaptation.

title: Trump makes one last attempt to get the Supreme Court to interfere with the midterms
excerpt: The Trump administration’s final bid to get the Supreme Court to interfere in the midterms, at least before Election Day, focuses on California. | Win McNamee/G
body: The Trump administration’s final bid to get the Supreme Court to interfere in the midterms, at least before Election Day, focuses on California. | Win McNamee/Getty Images Here’s a hot take: The outcome of the 2026 midterms is unlikely to turn on close races in California
California has no statewide races that are expected to be close, and it is a solid blue state that recently redrew its US House maps to maximize Democratic gains
So it’s a bit baffling that the Trump administration’s final bid to get the Supreme Court to interfere in the midterms, at least before Election Day, focuses on California

On Monday, the eve of the election, President Donald Trump’s Justice Department asked the justices to order California to “segregate” as many as 20,000 ballots and place them in a special pile where they may never be counted

The case emerges out of a list of over 20,000 names that the Trump administration first sent to California on October 13, asking election officials to separate their ballots and verify the voters’ eligibility
The administration claims that these individuals are “likely” noncitizens, but that they are nonetheless registered to vote in California
But it is unlikely that many — or even, potentially, any — of the names on this list are actually noncitizens who are registered to vote in California
Shortly after receiving Trump’s list, Los Angeles County officials took a sample of 200 names from the list to see if they are actually noncitizens who appear on the state’s voter rolls

In their preliminary review , they determined that nearly 40 percent of the names on the list belong to people who were born in the United States (and thus are almost certainly US citizens ), and that 56 percent of the individuals on the list either canceled their registration or their registration is no longer active
Over 70 percent have never voted in California
It is likely that further investigation will determine that even more of these individuals are either citizens or not actually registered to vote in California
This high error rate, moreover, closely mirrors a similar drama that played out earlier this year in Nevada

The Trump administration initially claimed that as many as 16,000 noncitizens appear on that state’s voter rolls, but when they later flagged a list of supposed noncitizen voters for Nevada officials, only 185 names appeared on the list
Nevada later determined that all 185 of these individuals are, in fact, citizens

So Trump wants the Supreme Court to interfere in the 2026 midterms based on a list of 20,000 names that is completely unreliable, and that may not identify a single actual person who is both registered to vote in California and a noncitizen
And even if all 20,000 of these individuals did cast a vote in the upcoming midterms, moreover, it is unlikely that they would change the result of any election
Just shy of 11 million people voted in California’s 2022 midterm elections, so the 20,000 people identified by Trump’s administration are a tiny fraction of the California electorate
And, on top of that, Trump’s lawyers are not even asking the Supreme Court to disenfranchise these 20,000 people — at least not yet
At this early stage of the litigation, Trump’s lawyers merely seek a court order requiring California to set these individuals’ ballots aside to determine if they are citizens or not
None of what Trump’s lawyers are asking for is legal
But the most striking thing about this case, which is known as United States v

Even if the justices agree with the Trump administration’s extra-legal claim that it can require a state to set aside ballots based on a highly dubious allegation that some of those ballots might belong to a noncitizen, that decision is unlikely to change the result of any 2026 election — although it could potentially allow this administration to sow chaos in 2028
Trump’s legal arguments are garbage Just in case there’s any doubt, there is absolutely no legal basis whatsoever for the Supreme Court to rule in favor of Trump’s administration
For starters, Trump’s lawyers rely on a statute which makes it a federal misdemeanor for some noncitizens to vote in a federal election
Notably, nothing in this statute regulates the state of California, or any other state
It does not prohibit state officials from counting any ballot, or require them to segregate any ballots into a special pile
This statute merely empowers the federal government to bring criminal charges against an individual noncitizen who votes illegally

If the Trump administration actually believes that any of the 20,000 names on its list are noncitizen voters, in other words, then its recourse is to gather enough evidence to prove, beyond a reasonable doubt, that one of those individuals violated federal law
Then it can charge that individual with a crime and potentially obtain a conviction
The statute simply does not permit federal courts to order segregation of ballots

Meanwhile, a separate federal law requires states to “complete, not later than 90 days prior to the date of a primary or general election for Federal office, any program the purpose of which is to systematically remove the names of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible voters.” So it’s actually illegal for California to comply with a request to remove the supposed noncitizens from its voter rolls, because this request came within 90 days of a federal election
Additionally, as the Supreme Court said less than two weeks ago in Scanlan v

Coalition for Open Democracy (2026), federal courts “should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election.” Trump’s lawyers filed their brief to the justices in the California case on the literal eve of an election

Finally, as Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, explained in an opinion arguing that Trump must lose this case , it is unlikely that California could comply with an order requiring it to segregate the contested ballots even if it wanted to

The state says that segregating these ballots “would be a logistical and administrative nightmare” because the list “does not contain the information necessary to identify voters; the Registrar has no established system for segregating ballots; and trying to create one now risks shutting down the system the Registrar needs to run the entire election.”  Additionally, Bennett writes, California “also lack[s] the ability to verify voters’ citizenship status before December 4, 2026—the deadline for counties to certify their election results to the Secretary of State.” Given these flaws in Trump’s case, it is unlikely that even this Supreme Court will order California to set aside the contested ballots
And, if Trump somehow does prevail, it is also unlikely that such a decision would change the result of any 2026 race

That said, in the unlikely event it does happen, a decision favoring Trump in California could allow him to interfere with the 2028 election — because it would enable the Trump administration to harass state election officials by sending them fabricated lists of “noncitizens” that the state would have to scramble to process while it was also trying to run an election.  But it is still unclear what Trump is trying to accomplish by bringing the California case to the justices on the day before an election , when even this Supreme Court is unlikely to rule in Trump’s favor
If this is the extent of Trump’s efforts to overturn an election that is expected to end badly for his Republican Party, then those efforts are unlikely to amount to anything at all.

title: A MAGA whisperer on why Republicans can still win
excerpt: President Donald Trump arrives on stage to deliver remarks during an election rally on October 25, 2026, in Port Huron, Michigan. | Alex Wong/Getty Images With
body: President Donald Trump arrives on stage to deliver remarks during an election rally on October 25, 2026, in Port Huron, Michigan. | Alex Wong/Getty Images With the midterms now upon us, polls continue to suggest that we’re headed for a blue wave election
One thing that might stop it is if Republican voters come out in big numbers on Election Day

But is MAGA even united behind their candidates? And do they have a plan to motivate a base that seems to be souring on a second Trump administration?  Conservative radio host John Fredericks, a longtime Trump supporter whose show offers a window into the MAGA mindset, thinks the GOP can pull off a victory
Fredericks acknowledges that affordability is a real issue for Republicans, who triumphed in 2024 with promises to improve an economy that they haven’t been able to turn around
But he sees Trump as a closer — capable of stepping in at the last minute, firing up his supporters, and helping Republicans pull off an upset
America, Actually host Astead Herndon spoke with Fredericks about both the financial pressures that voters are feeling and why they might not matter for the president’s most ardent supporters
Fredericks argues that things are improving — and thinks voters know it

He also shared his predictions about how Republicans might pull ahead in the Senate and offered three elections to watch that could be early bellwethers on election night.  Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
You are in touch with Republican voters and folks in the administration
I think you represent the kind of voice of that MAGA community
In that world, what is the final argument for the midterms? Stay the course
The underpinnings of the economy are phenomenal
Everything we’re doing, they’re off the charts
People don’t spend their money if they don’t think things are going to go well in the future
You put a college football game on a Saturday
That doesn’t mean that they’re not pissed because of gas, they’re not upset because of groceries
Everybody’s upset over the cost of living and gas and diesel

And that’s a real problem.  But at the end of the day, jobs are up, wages are up, and I think our voters, our Trump voters, are going to be patient enough to wait this out.  Look, he had to go into Iran
Obviously, he got intel there that they were too close to getting a bomb, deploying it on a ballistic missile
If they did that, what [would] gas be now, what [would] oil be? Would it be $90 a barrel? It would be $400 a barrel
They’d have the whole world hostage.  President Trump, after five decades, made the decision with Iran
I hear that, but the last inflation report before the election showed that consumer prices are up 3.7 percent year to year
You have gas hovering at about $4 nationally
As we both know, the fundamental promise of this administration was about lowering prices
They were pointing to things like grocery prices, meat prices

They were pointing to gas prices under Biden.  Can’t we at least acknowledge that Trump has not followed through on his promises on that front? If affordability was not an issue, the Republicans would win this election in a landslide
Things are too expensive for people, and having the interest rates go up doesn’t help either
I go to the store with my family, we feel it

I appreciate that you’re saying that, because we’re hearing a lot of Republican candidates basically say, “Well, Biden was worse.” But we’re talking about right now.  The closing argument here is the fundamentals are getting better
And certainly his decision to stop Iran from getting a bomb from the intel that he got from our intel agencies [matters]
We don’t know how far Iran would be now had he not done that
So President Trump had to make that decision
The MAGA base is there.  This argument that the MAGA base is crumbling is coming from right-wing clickbaiters
And you know who clicks on them? The Democrats
This is the doom loop, right? It’s all doom
It’s all gloom.  Even you are acknowledging a slight affordability problem for this administration
You’re acknowledging that the Iran war is going to cost the party some seats
So can we say that this is all made up by doom grifters? It’s not slight, it’s real.  I’m not disagreeing on the affordability issue or the gas or diesel prices or the price of meat

The fundamental thing is, are MAGA voters going to stay home and abandon the president?  The Trump voters [are] going to turn out, and I think they’re going to give this president the benefit of the doubt

title: The Supreme Court could make it impossible to sue federal officers
excerpt: Law enforcement officers detain an activist outside the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building during a protest opposing ICE operations, in Minneapolis on March
body: Law enforcement officers detain an activist outside the Bishop Henry Whipple Federal Building during a protest opposing ICE operations, in Minneapolis on March 1, 2026. | Kerem Yucel/AFP via Getty Images Let’s say that you’re savagely beaten by a federal officer despite the fact that you committed no crime
Or maybe your home is ransacked by FBI agents who didn’t even bother to get a warrant
Or maybe you’re shot in cold blood by immigration officials engaged in a paramilitary occupation of your home city
The Supreme Court has worked hard, especially in recent years, to ensure that you will have little, if any, recourse against federal law enforcement officials who abuse their power
In one case, decided about six years ago, the Court’s Republican majority gave lawsuit immunity to a US Border Patrol agent who fatally shot a Mexican teenager in the face
Now, the Court is poised to finish the job
On November 9, the Court will hear Nielsen v
Watanabe , a case that could eliminate all remaining hope that someone targeted by a federal officer with no regard for the Constitution might be able to hold that officer accountable in court
Among other things, the justices could use Nielsen to overrule its decision in Bivens v
Six Unknown Named Agents (1971), which established that federal law enforcement officers may sometimes be sued if they violate someone’s constitutional rights
Bivens was rooted in something very similar to the Spider-Man Rule — with great power comes great responsibility

As the Court explained in Bivens , a federal officer who acts unlawfully “in the name of the United States possesses a far greater capacity for harm than an individual trespasser exercising no authority other than his own.” And thus the Constitution must offer some remedy to people who are injured by such an officer
But Bivens quickly fell out of favor in the Supreme Court as its membership moved rightward
The Court’s current, Republican majority is so unrelentingly hostile toward Bivens that it is hard to imagine any plaintiff prevailing in a Bivens suit before this Court

The Court’s most recent decisions have described Bivens suits as a “disfavored judicial activity.” In one decision, they’ve said that it is “ doubtful that we would have reached the same result ” if Bivens were “decided today.” And they’ve instructed judges to reject Bivens claims if there is “ any rational reason (even one) ” to do so
In Nielsen , the same justices who wrote these lines are now being asked to overrule Bivens altogether
Even if they decide not to go that far, they’ve already done so much to carve up Bivens that there is virtually no hope for anyone who sues a federal officer for violating their constitutional rights

What’s the specific issue in Nielsen ? Nielsen arises out of an alleged violation of the Eighth Amendment, which forbids “ cruel and unusual punishments .” The Supreme Court has long held that this amendment requires prisons to provide medical care to incarcerated people , because if the prison does not provide them with care, they will have no other way to treat their illnesses or injuries
The last time the Court ruled in favor of someone who sued a federal officer under Bivens was Carlson v
Green (1980), a decision that allowed the estate of a man who died in prison due to poor medical care to sue prison officials under Bivens
The Nielsen plaintiff, a formerly incarcerated man named Kekai Watanabe, raises a similar claim to the one in Carlson
Watanabe was assaulted by fellow inmates, and received some medical care for “severe back pain.” But when he asked to be treated in a hospital, that care was denied
He claims that, for months, he “received only intermittent and short-term treatment for pain, often over-the-counter medication,” despite repeated requests for more care

After seven months, according to his brief, Watanabe was finally given an X-ray, which revealed that he had a fractured tailbone and that “bone chips had migrated into the surrounding soft tissue.” Watanabe also claims that he was never given treatment by a medical specialist, and “ remains in tremendous pain today .” A federal appeals court concluded that Watanabe’s legal claim “is identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects,” and thus his lawsuit against a prison health provider could move forward

Though the Supreme Court “has cautioned against extending Bivens remedies,” the lower court explained, “it has consistently maintained that” Carlson is “still good law.” On the one hand, the appeals court is correct that Watanabe alleges a legal violation that is very similar to the one in Carlson
In both cases, someone incarcerated in a federal prison alleged that their Eighth Amendment rights were violated because the prison did not provide them with adequate medical care
So that does suggest that Watanabe should be allowed to bring a Bivens claim for as long as Carlson remains good law
Still, the Court’s recent cases tell judges to rule against Bivens plaintiffs if there is “ any rational reason ” to do so
And there are certainly some distinctions that can be drawn between Carlson and Nielsen
The plaintiff in Carlson , for example, had an asthma attack and died within hours , while Watanabe is still alive and his medical condition played out over many months
The defendants’ lawyers in Nielsen also argue that Congress has changed the law governing suits brought by federal prisoners in ways that make their case meaningfully different from Carlson
But if judges are really supposed to look for any rational reason to deny Bivens claims, then these distinctions are almost certainly enough
Again, it’s hard to imagine this Supreme Court ruling in favor of any Bivens plaintiff, including Watanabe
In Nielsen , the lawyers asking the Court to overrule Bivens claim that, since Carlson , the Court has rejected 13 different suits raising Bivens arguments
For what it is worth, the legal debate over Bivens focuses on whether Congress must specifically authorize suits against federal officers before those suits can move forward

The Court’s Republicans claim that the absence of such a law means that no suits against federal officers are allowed (a federal law does authorize suits against state officials who violate constitutional rights ).  Meanwhile, proponents of Bivens argue that the 1971 decision merely added coherence to a long line of pre- Bivens decisions permitting suits against federal officials — some of which stretch back to the early 1800s

Domestic & Foreign Commerce Corp. (1949), “the principle that an agent is liable for his own torts ‘is an ancient one and applies even to certain acts of public officers or public instrumentalities.’” But it matters little who is correct about this debate, because Republicans control six seats on the Supreme Court, and those six justices are fully dug into their opposition to Bivens
The biggest open question in Nielsen , in other words, is whether the Court will take the defendant’s lawyers up on their invitation to overrule Bivens in its entirety
Just a few years ago, a decision overruling Bivens would have been a very big deal
But, in light of the Court’s decisions holding that judges should look for reasons to deny Bivens claims, little of Bivens remains to be further undermined by this Court

title: Gen Z can’t afford the culture war
excerpt: Attendees hold signs during a campaign event with state Rep
body: Attendees hold signs during a campaign event with state Rep

Claire Valdez in Brooklyn, New York, on June 22, 2026. | Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images Conventional wisdom holds that young voters are idealistic and socially progressive dreamers, while older voters are hard-headed, pragmatic, and much more attuned to pocketbook issues.  Conventional wisdom, meet Gen Z

Between 2020 and 2024, voters in this cohort swung right by more than 20 percentage points — but now they’re boomeranging back away from President Donald Trump, mainly over the cost of living and a deep sense of economic anxiety, according to a number of recent surveys of young voters. “Inflation/prices” is the top concern for voters under 30 in YouGov’s “most important issue” tracker , far above civil rights and civil liberties

The cost of living, corruption, and US involvement in foreign conflict were the top three issues for young Americans 18–29 (who say they have at least a 50-50 chance of voting in the midterm elections) in this fall’s Harvard IOP youth poll, with 65 percent of this cohort saying the cost of living is “extremely important” in determining their midterm vote

Similarly, 49 percent of the same young Americans in the poll said their personal finances have gotten worse since Trump took office for a second term and 91 percent said the cost of living will be “important in determining their vote.” The final New York Times/Siena national poll of the midterms reported 0 percent of likely voters under 30 “strongly approve” of Trump’s performance on cost-of-living issues. “ It’s the economy, stupid ” is not a new observation in politics, but the fact that Gen Z voters are prioritizing the economy above social issues marks a genuine shift from their earlier habits
As recently as 2020, healthcare, the environment and climate change, and racism topped young voters’ priorities, according to Gallup

Back then, 79 percent of youth told pollsters that the pandemic helped them realize how much politicians’ decisions affected their lives, which added a unique society-wide issue that often didn’t fit into traditional economic categories

And in the 2022 midterm cycle, Gen Z voters were the only age group to name abortion as the top concern in deciding their vote, ranking the issue 23 points higher than inflation in a Tufts University CIRCLE analysis of national exit-poll data.  Not anymore
What Gen Z wants from elections Call it the post-culture war

Just two years ago, Trump returned to the White House in part thanks to anti-woke “manosphere” influencers popular with young men, even as young women became more liberal , especially on issues like the environment and abortion.  Now, as the top issues are changing, there’s more consensus: Amid an AI revolution, rising inflation, and war in the Middle East, identity politics can feel like a luxury
Young women were actually more likely than young men to say that rising prices and inflation constitute “an urgent crisis requiring immediate action,” in the spring Harvard IOP youth poll
The implications are potentially far-reaching — and not just for the midterms
Both parties will need to reckon with a rising generation consumed by cost-of-living concerns in ways that could challenge the status quo and force new compromises with older generations

Already housing has become a familiar flashpoint: Young voters feel locked out of buying a home, but what might help reduce prices for them could be seen as a plan to reduce property values for older voters sitting on a home they bought long ago

And on healthcare, both parties could face more pressure to help younger voters grappling with surging costs in employer and individual insurance plans, which could compete for federal dollars and attention with programs for seniors like Medicare.  Lately, I’m hearing young people describe frustration with candidates for a focus on policies that feel tailored to boomers or Gen X, such as raising taxes to fund Social Security or slashing property taxes for existing homeowners, without much attention on remedies for young Americans in the short term, such as bringing down the cost of rent, making higher education more affordable, or increasing healthcare options for younger Americans unable to get a job

In my focus groups with young voters, the economic anxiety is palpable. “I feel like over the last year things definitely have changed,” a 21-year-old man from Miami said. “You see it generally even with gas prices…a lot of it has to do with the fact that our country has involved itself in a lot of different conflicts around the world at this point.” Meanwhile, asked about the top political or social issue impacting her right now, a 23-year-old woman from Tucson, Arizona, said the price of everything felt too high: “The rising cost of living
Everything just feels more expensive like groceries, rent, gas…even as a college student last year

And healthcare is a big concern.” And a 21-year-old student in Pennsylvania said he uses student loan refunds to finance daily necessities.  “During the school year, I am relying on my refunds from school to pay my rent, to pay my car payment and car insurance, phone bill, internet, stuff like that,” he told me, adding, “right now, my focus is on economic issues because I feel that I need to continue working simply just to live, that I don’t have much room to focus on cultural issues, since what is on my mind is how I will be getting my next meal

Which then ties in cultural issues, but the main forefront is the economic issues.” What changed for young voters?  One interpretation for why younger Gen Z voters are putting economics ahead of cultural issues is simple: The economic outlook for young people is frightening, with constant talk of new technology transforming — or eliminating — the careers they hoped to pursue.  One study found that employment among workers ages 22–25 in AI-exposed occupations was 19 percent lower than it would have been had it kept pace with their less-exposed peers — a gap that has widened since researchers first reported it in August 2025
Another found that only 30 percent of 2025 college graduates got a full-time job related to their degree (an 11-point drop from 2024)
So it’s no shock that today, the majority of adults under 30 are more concerned than excited about AI, according to the Pew Research Center
Meanwhile, just 63 percent of adults 18–29 said they are “doing okay” or “living comfortably,” which is notably lower than the 83 percent of adults 60 and over who say the same
Anecdotally, I often hear young people say that they feel like they’re worse off economically than their parents were at the same age
These are difficult claims to check, both individually and in aggregate

But a lot of it comes down to homeownership and the sense of financial stability that comes along with it, which feels like an impossible dream for many in Gen Z. “Obviously cultural and those other issues are important, but at the end of the day the most important thing is putting food on the table, gas in the car, and the roof over your head,” a 26-year-old teacher from Illinois told me. “And it feels right now like that’s kinda impossible to do all three
You can put gas in the car and food in your stomach but it’s hard to find a house or apartment to rent or buy

It’s kinda like Maslow’s hierarchy of needs where if your core issues aren’t satisfied you can’t look higher up the pyramid.” Millennials who came of age during the Great Recession might find this all familiar
And in fact, in 2008, the Harvard IOP youth poll found that the economy was the top issue for young Americans ages 18–24

Of course, worrying about the economy and voting on the economy are two separate things, and young voters — who turned out in 2008 at much higher rates than prior presidential years — will need to be convinced by politicians that it’s worth putting their trust in elections to help, let alone either party.  The post-2024 CIRCLE poll of young people offers one interesting wrinkle in this regard

Those who didn’t vote were more likely than those who did to name inflation and the cost of living, as well as jobs and unemployment, among their top three priorities. (The 2024 election also saw lower youth turnout compared to 2020 — about 47 percent versus 50 percent, respectively.) We’ll see if that dynamic changes this midterm cycle

When voters transition from voting on social and cultural issues to voting based on economic ones, it’s often said condescendingly that they’re voting with their “heads” rather than their “hearts” or that they’re “growing up” and learning that running a household takes more money and responsibility than they expected
I don’t think these young adults are growing up; I think they’re freaking out.

title: Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
excerpt: Eating disorders are surging globally: A new study in JAMA Psychiatry found anorexia and bulimia rose 71% between 1990 and 2023, affecting an estimated 18.1 mil
body: Eating disorders are surging globally: A new study in JAMA Psychiatry found anorexia and bulimia rose 71% between 1990 and 2023, affecting an estimated 18.1 million people—and experts say the true number affected by eating disorders is likely three times higher

Social media is fueling the crisis: TikTok's algorithm served users with eating disorders 4,343% more harmful content than those without—and clinicians say "thinspiration" trends can trigger new cases

GLP-1 drugs are making things worse: Experts are already seeing patients—some as young as 11—misusing weight-loss drugs " data-chronoton-post-id="1147838" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade
But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders
A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%
By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders
What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders
And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue
Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years
She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says
Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health
They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others
It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset
That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny
Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson
Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the  heroin chic era springs to mind)

To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world
The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps
That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023
They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one  DALY represents a year of healthy life lost)
The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling
Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found
Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too
In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai
Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise
In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people
Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study
The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says
Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth)

So how did we get here? Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study
Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says

Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or “fitspiration” content
But users with eating disorders appear to be more likely to engage with this content—and to be fed more of it as a result

When researchers at the University of Melbourne  investigated this phenomenon a couple of years ago, they found that the algorithms of TikTok users with eating disorders delivered 4343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” than those of users who didn’t have the disorders
They also got more content focused on dieting or exercising
Many were fed over 1000 problematic videos per month
Bulik describes social media as “quicksand” for people with, or at risk of, eating disorders
The covid-19 pandemic—and the social isolation that accompanied lockdowns—also appears to have contributed to the rise in eating disorders
Research conducted in 2021 found that the number of people hospitalized with eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020
Researchers don’t yet have good data on how trends in eating disorders might have progressed since 2023

body: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country

body: Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths , Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies

body: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days
